entries.use: Describe an intended culmination while naming the emotions and unresolved elements more specifically.
entries.example: Two estranged siblings finally acknowledge their shared grief without solving the practical dispute that separated them.

entries.name: Identification
entries.definition: A viewer's sense of connection or alignment with a character's situation, goals, perspective, or imagined position. It can shift during a story and differs from literal identity or unqualified approval.
entries.use: Consider which experiences invite the viewer to accompany a character and which create friction.
entries.example: We share an outsider's difficulty understanding station rules even while noticing that she treats other passengers unfairly.

entries.name: Emotional distance
entries.definition: The degree to which presentation encourages detached observation, reflection, or evaluation instead of immediate emotional closeness. It is an interpretive quality, not something determined solely by shot size.
entries.use: Give viewers room to consider patterns, contradictions, or institutions beyond one person's reaction.
entries.example: An uninterrupted wide shot lets us observe several passengers' competing needs during an argument rather than privileging one face.

entries.name: Withheld information
entries.definition: Relevant information that presentation leaves unavailable for a period. What is withheld may be obvious to the audience as a question or may become apparent only after disclosure.
entries.use: Specify the information gap and its duration, keeping it consistent with the established presentation.
entries.example: We hear one side of a telephone call and learn the other speaker's identity only when the call ends.

entries.name: Dramatic irony
entries.definition: A knowledge difference that lets the audience interpret a character's words or actions beyond the character's own understanding. This is a relationship between perspectives rather than a tone in itself.
entries.use: Make a familiar action carry an additional implication for the viewer.
entries.example: We have seen the canceled departure notice while a traveler reassures her family that she will arrive tonight.

entries.name: Point-of-view shot
entries.definition: A shot presented as approximately what a particular character sees, commonly established by surrounding shots or staging. It need not reproduce human vision with optical precision.
entries.use: Tie a visible detail to a character's attention while distinguishing seeing from understanding.
entries.example: After the passenger looks down the track, a view along it reveals a stationary lantern in the distance.

entries.name: Reaction shot
entries.definition: A shot emphasizing a response to an event, statement, or perceived object. A response can be a slight change, deliberate restraint, or apparent absence of reaction.
entries.use: Give the audience access to consequences and interpretation through behavior.
entries.example: After an announcement names a destination, the camera stays with the one passenger who stops packing.

entries.name: Observational perspective
entries.definition: A descriptive approach that lets behavior and situations unfold with an emphasis on watching and listening rather than overt explanation. It is not automatically the documentary mode called observational cinema.
entries.use: Make time, routine, and relationships available for the audience's own inference.
entries.example: We spend a passage watching a cleaner prepare the closed station, learning its rhythms before any problem is announced.

entries.name: Subtext
entries.definition: Meaning, desire, or tension communicated beneath the literal words. Subtext may emerge through context, delivery, avoidance, or contradictory behavior; it does not require a consciously hidden message in every line.
entries.use: Give a conversation more than one level while preserving playable intentions. The National Theatre's rehearsal discussion connects subtext to what speakers seek from one another. [National Theatre, *Three Sisters* rehearsal pack](https://images.nationaltheatre.org.uk/uploads/2022/10/BPA-three-sisters-pack.pdf).
entries.example: “You kept the receipt?” sounds practical, but the speaker is testing whether the gift was chosen reluctantly.

entries.name: Exposition
entries.definition: Information that helps the audience understand circumstances, relationships, history, or rules. In dialogue, exposition is spoken information; it can also be carried by action and design elsewhere in the film.
entries.use: Supply what the scene needs without making characters explain facts solely for the viewer. Give the information a present purpose, such as persuasion or correction.
entries.example: A tenant refuses the landlord's offer: “You promised repairs before last winter, too.”

entries.name: Banter
entries.definition: A conversational exchange built around playful challenge, teasing, or quick replies. Its surface lightness can coexist with affection, competitiveness, resentment, or unequal permission to joke.
entries.use: Establish relational familiarity and verbal rhythm. Distinguish mutual play from a situation in which one person laughs only to remain accepted.
entries.example: Two mechanics trade jokes about each other's repairs until one mentions a failed inspection and the other stops smiling.

entries.name: Monologue
entries.definition: An extended stretch of speech by one person. Other characters may be present and listening; a monologue is not necessarily a soliloquy, direct address, or narration.
entries.use: Sustain a particular viewpoint while allowing changes in tactic, thought, and listener response to provide movement within the speech.
entries.example: A retiring conductor recounts a railway accident, first entertaining the room, then gradually admitting his own responsibility.

entries.name: Interruption
entries.definition: An event that cuts into an ongoing utterance or action. Another speaker, a sound, or the original speaker's self-correction can interrupt; sustained simultaneous speech is not required.
entries.use: Change conversational control, prevent information from landing, or show urgent recognition. Specify the trigger so the timing can be repeated across takes.
entries.example: Before a witness names the visitor, the lawyer cuts in with a question about the weather.

entries.name: Overlap
entries.definition: Two or more voices sounding at the same time. Overlap may result from interruption, agreement, a shared routine, or competing conversations; it is an audible relationship, not automatically a conflict.
entries.use: Build group texture or urgency while deciding which words must remain intelligible. Sound recording and editorial flexibility affect how it is staged.
entries.example: Siblings finish different versions of the same family story over one another.

entries.name: Silence
entries.definition: The absence of speech during a meaningful interval. Performance silence may still contain breathing, movement, environmental sound, music, and active thought; it does not imply an empty soundtrack.
entries.use: Let a question remain unanswered, allow attention to shift, or make nonverbal behavior carry a choice. Its meaning depends on preceding and subsequent action.
entries.example: Offered an apology, a shopkeeper quietly turns the sign from open to closed.

entries.name: Understatement
entries.definition: Expression that deliberately gives less verbal or emotional emphasis than the circumstances might conventionally invite. It differs from simply lacking clarity or failing to respond.
entries.use: Suggest control, social convention, humor, or an attempt to contain feeling. The surrounding evidence must let the audience perceive what has been reduced.
entries.example: Surveying a flooded kitchen, the homeowner says, “We may need another towel,” while lifting a floating chair.

entries.name: Naturalistic performance
entries.definition: Acting organized to resemble plausible everyday behavior within the work's social and aesthetic conventions. Hesitation, interruption, and subtle response may contribute, but no checklist makes a performance naturalistic.
entries.use: Encourage attention to believable circumstances and relationships. Naturalism is constructed and rehearsable; it does not mean the actor simply behaves as themselves.
entries.example: A cashier continues sorting coins while trying to conceal concern about an unexpected visitor.

entries.name: Stylized performance
entries.definition: Acting that uses an evident formal pattern beyond ordinary behavioral imitation, such as choreographed gestures, patterned speech, or deliberately artificial timing.
entries.use: Establish a coherent performance language for satire, ritual, fantasy, or other forms. Consistency among performers can matter more than resemblance to daily conversation.
entries.example: Every official in a fictional ministry repeats the same precise hand movement before delivering a refusal.

entries.name: Restrained performance
entries.definition: Acting with limited outward display relative to the character's situation or the production's baseline. Emotion and intention remain active even when vocal and physical changes are small.
entries.use: Make minor departures from habitual behavior consequential. Camera distance, sound, and editing need to preserve the details on which the performance depends.
entries.example: A normally meticulous archivist misaligns one folder after learning that her colleague has disappeared.

entries.name: Heightened performance
entries.definition: Acting whose vocal, physical, or emotional expression is amplified beyond a production's ordinary register. It can still follow psychologically coherent intentions and need not become caricature.
entries.use: Meet the expressive demands of melodrama, farce, musical scenes, or moments of rupture. Define the baseline so intensity has a recognizable relationship to the surrounding work.
entries.example: A mayor's ceremonial confidence swells into theatrical outrage when the audience begins laughing.

entries.name: Deadpan
entries.definition: Delivery that maintains a notably matter-of-fact or unexpressive surface despite surprising, absurd, or emotionally charged content. Deadpan is a specific contrast between presentation and circumstances.
entries.use: Let the audience perceive incongruity without an actor visibly announcing the joke. It can also suggest habit, concealment, or institutional indifference.
entries.example: A hotel clerk calmly adds “minor ceiling collapse” to a guest's list of room preferences.

entries.name: Vocal rhythm
entries.definition: The pattern of speech timing, stress, duration, and phrasing across an utterance. Rhythm includes variation and rests; it is more specific than speaking quickly or slowly.
entries.use: Differentiate thought processes, relationships, or changes of tactic. A rhythmic shift may matter more than the overall pace.
entries.example: A negotiator speaks in clipped units while reading terms, then lengthens the final phrase when asking for trust.

entries.name: Pause
entries.definition: A temporary break within speech or action. A pause has a position and duration relative to something continuing; silence is the broader condition of not speaking.
entries.use: Mark reconsideration, a withheld response, or time needed to register information. Give the performer a reason for the pause rather than only a prescribed delay.
entries.example: A sister pauses before saying “our house,” deciding whether to include her estranged brother.

entries.name: Breath
entries.definition: The audible or visible pattern of inhalation, exhalation, and breath suspension within a performance. Breath supports voice and can reveal effort, anticipation, regulation, or a change of thought.
entries.use: Connect speech to physical action and let transitions occur before words arrive. Avoid treating any single breathing pattern as proof of a particular emotion.
entries.example: A runner steadies her breathing before recording a message that claims everything is ordinary.

entries.name: Volume
entries.definition: The relative loudness of a performer's vocal delivery. Performance volume and the final soundtrack level are related but distinct: a whispered line can be mixed prominently.
entries.use: Establish who must hear, who might overhear, and how effort changes during a scene. Discuss vocal behavior separately from microphone placement or playback loudness.
entries.example: A parent lowers their voice as an argument reaches the doorway of a sleeping child's room.

entries.name: Gesture
entries.definition: A meaningful or expressive bodily movement, often involving hands, arms, face, or head. A gesture can be deliberate communication, habitual action, or behavior whose significance the character does not recognize.
entries.use: Externalize a tactic or reveal contradiction without making every movement symbolic. Consider cultural context and continuity across coverage.
entries.example: A candidate verbally welcomes questions while repeatedly guiding the interviewer toward the exit.

entries.name: Posture
entries.definition: The body's sustained alignment or attitude in space, including how weight, spine, shoulders, and head are organized. Posture is a condition that may change, whereas a gesture is a movement.
entries.use: Express occupation, fatigue, habit, or a relationship to the room without reducing personality to a body type.
entries.example: A retired soldier initially stands through a meeting, then finally accepts the chair offered by his daughter.

entries.name: Eyeline
entries.definition: The direction and apparent target of a character's gaze. In production, an eyeline also identifies where a performer should look so shots describe a coherent spatial relationship.
entries.use: Establish attention, avoidance, or an unseen presence. Match target height and screen direction when coverage requires continuity; looking at the lens creates a different relationship.
entries.example: A witness answers the detective but watches the reflection of someone behind him.

entries.name: Blocking
entries.definition: The planned positions, movements, and physical interactions of performers through a scene. It includes relationships to furniture, props, entrances, and camera coverage, rather than merely marks on the floor.
entries.use: Turn dramatic changes into spatial events and coordinate repeatable action. Rehearsal can discover blocking as well as execute a predetermined plan.
entries.example: Each failed request moves a daughter farther from the dinner table until her mother must stand to continue speaking.

entries.name: Entrance
entries.definition: A character's arrival into a scene, playing area, or visible frame. Entering the room and entering the camera's frame may occur at different moments.
entries.use: Control when presence becomes known and how it alters an existing arrangement. An entrance can be announced by sound before anyone becomes visible.
entries.example: Work boots appear beneath the office door before the employee hears that the building owner has arrived.

entries.name: Exit
entries.definition: A character's departure from the scene's space or from the visible frame. An off-screen character may remain nearby and continue influencing the action.
entries.use: End participation, transfer attention, or leave an unresolved relationship behind. Specify whether the departure is geographical, conversational, or simply outside the shot.
entries.example: A manager leaves the frame, but her keys remain on the table and her voice continues from the corridor.

entries.name: Crossing
entries.definition: A performer's movement from one position to another across the playing space or frame. A cross can alter sightlines and relationships even when dialogue continues uninterrupted.
entries.use: Make a tactic physical, reveal or conceal another subject, and create opportunities for reframing. Mark start, destination, and dramatic trigger.
entries.example: While denying interest in the letter, a guest crosses from the fireplace to the desk where it lies.

entries.name: Proximity
entries.definition: The closeness of characters to one another or to a significant object. Its meaning depends on personal, cultural, spatial, and situational expectations rather than a universal distance scale.
entries.use: Explore access, trust, intimidation, or practical cooperation. Record actual distance only when measurement helps reproduce the staging.
entries.example: Two rivals must lean toward the same failing radio, briefly sharing a space they have otherwise avoided.

entries.name: Separation
entries.definition: Spatial distance or an intervening boundary between participants. Separation can exist despite physical closeness when furniture, orientation, or another body prevents contact and shared attention.
entries.use: Make a relationship legible through space while leaving its interpretation open to context. A divided arrangement can precede reconciliation or protect a character's privacy.
entries.example: A glass partition lets a mother and son see each other but prevents their attempted embrace.

entries.name: Stillness
entries.definition: A sustained reduction of visible bodily movement. Stillness can contain intense attention, preparation, resistance, or exhaustion; it is not equivalent to inactivity or emotional emptiness.
entries.use: Create contrast with surrounding motion or make a small change readable. Distinguish intentional stillness from freezing because a performer has no playable action.
entries.example: As everyone rushes to pack, one resident remains seated with the house key resting in her palm.

entries.name: Group arrangement
entries.definition: The spatial organization of several people, including clusters, rows, gaps, orientation, and shared or competing centers of attention. It describes collective blocking rather than only individual positions.
entries.use: Show affiliation and access without explanatory dialogue. Track how the arrangement changes when someone enters, defects, or becomes the focus.
entries.example: Workers begin in separate lunch groups and gradually form one semicircle around a dismissed colleague.

entries.name: Objective
entries.definition: What a character wants to achieve in a particular stretch of action. A useful performance objective concerns an outcome, often involving another person, rather than an instruction to display an emotion.
entries.use: Give speech and movement direction while permitting multiple tactics. Scene objectives can conflict with a character's wider goals or stated intentions.
entries.example: During a farewell, the visitor's immediate objective is to make the host ask them to stay.

entries.name: Tactic
entries.definition: A specific approach a character uses to pursue an objective, such as persuading, flattering, challenging, distracting, or reassuring. Tactics can change while the desired outcome remains constant.
entries.use: Replace vague emotional instructions with actions aimed at a partner. The National Theatre describes such work through what speakers try to elicit from each other. [*Three Sisters* rehearsal pack](https://images.nationaltheatre.org.uk/uploads/2022/10/BPA-three-sisters-pack.pdf).
entries.example: To borrow the van, a brother first jokes, then bargains, then admits why he needs it.

entries.name: Listening
entries.definition: Active reception and interpretation of another person's words and behavior within a performance. Listening can change the listener's next action before any spoken response occurs.
entries.use: Keep exchanges responsive rather than making each actor wait for a cue. The National Theatre's rehearsal account emphasizes attention to the acting partner. [*Three Sisters* rehearsal pack](https://images.nationaltheatre.org.uk/uploads/2022/10/BPA-three-sisters-pack.pdf).
entries.example: A prepared objection disappears when the speaker hears an unexpectedly personal reason for the decision.

entries.name: Reaction
entries.definition: A response to perceived information, action, or sensation. It can be vocal, physical, delayed, suppressed, or displaced into another task; it is not restricted to a facial expression.
entries.use: Show that an event has changed someone's internal or practical situation. Distinguish the performed response from a reaction shot, which is a framing or editorial function.
entries.example: Hearing a familiar name, a cook turns off the burner before asking who called.

entries.name: Status shift
entries.definition: A change in the relative authority, influence, or social position enacted between participants. Immediate interactional status can differ from formal rank and can reverse within a single exchange.
entries.use: Identify the moment behavior reorganizes around a new source of power. Look for altered permission, space, interruption patterns, or who seeks whose approval.
entries.example: The inspector stops asking questions when the cleaner reveals she has the only copy of the report.

entries.name: Set design
entries.definition: The conception and specification of spaces built or adapted for filming, including layout, architecture, surfaces, and functional requirements. A set may be physical, virtual, or a planned combination.
entries.use: Shape the possibilities for action and camera placement while expressing the story's world. Production designers coordinate design with construction, decoration, props, and other departments. [ScreenSkills, production designer skills](https://www.screenskills.com/skills-checklists/scripted-film-and-tv/art-department/production-designer-skills/).
entries.example: A records office is designed with narrow public counters and a vast archive visible behind them.

entries.name: Location dressing
entries.definition: Adding, removing, covering, or rearranging visible elements at an existing filming location to suit the story. It adapts a found environment rather than necessarily building its underlying architecture.
entries.use: Transform a suitable place into a specific fictional one while working with existing geometry and access. The term overlaps with set dressing but identifies the location context.
entries.example: A contemporary café receives older signs, period tableware, and coverings over electronic payment terminals.

entries.name: Props
entries.definition: Objects selected or made for use within the action, especially objects handled by performers. “Properties” is the longer form; boundaries with dressing and costume vary across departments and productions.
entries.use: Give characters practical actions and make plot information tangible. ScreenSkills distinguishes handled objects from the environmental focus of set decoration. [ScreenSkills, set decorator](https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/craft/set-decorator/).
entries.example: A dented lunchbox carries the note that changes a factory worker's decision.

entries.name: Hero prop
entries.definition: A featured object, or a specially detailed version of an object, intended for prominent scrutiny or important action. “Hero” describes production emphasis and does not mean the object belongs to a heroic character.
entries.use: Identify items needing readable detail, dependable interaction, close-up finish, or matching duplicates. Distinguish a display-quality version from stunt or background versions where relevant.
entries.example: A brass compass has a working engraved dial for the scene in which its hidden inscription is discovered.

entries.name: Set dressing
entries.definition: The furnishings, decoration, and environmental objects arranged to give a set its specific character and history. Dressing may include furniture, textiles, wall objects, and background clutter.
entries.use: Communicate how a place is occupied and maintained without requiring dialogue. A dressing item may need coordination with props if it becomes part of performed action. [ScreenSkills, set decorator](https://www.screenskills.com/job-profiles/browse/film-and-tv-drama/craft/set-decorator/).
entries.example: Repeated replacement chair legs suggest that a boarding house repairs possessions instead of replacing them.

entries.name: Practical fixture
entries.definition: A functioning fixture within the designed environment, most commonly a visible lamp or other light source. In broader art-department usage, “practical” can also indicate that a door, tap, or device actually operates.
entries.use: Let performers interact with the environment and provide visible motivation for illumination. A practical lamp may be supplemented by lights outside the frame.
entries.example: A desk lamp switches on during a confession while concealed lighting helps its apparent beam illuminate the listener.

entries.name: Costume
entries.definition: Clothing and wearable accessories chosen or constructed for a character, including their fit, condition, and changes through the story. Contemporary everyday clothing is costume when deliberately selected for the production.
entries.use: Express circumstances, self-presentation, occupation, or transformation while supporting movement and continuity. Clothing should work with the performer and scene rather than function only as a symbolic label.
entries.example: A character wears an interview jacket with the temporary sleeve stitching still attached.

entries.name: Makeup
entries.definition: Cosmetic and corrective or transformative work applied to a performer's visible appearance. It may create an intentionally ordinary result, a stylized design, or a changing physical condition.
entries.use: Support characterization and camera rendering while maintaining a documented progression across scenes. Makeup is distinct from the full wardrobe, hairstyle, and any separate prosthetic appliances.
entries.example: Carefully tracked fading bruises help show that several story days have passed between scenes shot out of order.

entries.name: Hair
entries.definition: The design and maintenance of a character's hairstyle, facial hair, wigs, and related hairpieces. Decisions include shape, grooming, texture, movement, and condition rather than only color or length.
entries.use: Establish routine, period, chosen presentation, and continuity across a story. Coordinate movement and silhouette with costume and camera tests.
entries.example: A meticulously pinned hairstyle loosens gradually during a long overnight shift, with each stage recorded for later coverage.

entries.name: Prosthetics
entries.definition: Applied pieces that alter a performer's apparent anatomy or surface, such as sculpted appliances for age, injury, creatures, or other transformations. In this context the term concerns performance makeup effects.
entries.use: Create repeatable three-dimensional changes that interact with light and movement. Design must consider expression, application, removal, and the needs of the performer.
entries.example: A subtle silicone cheek appliance gives a fictional survivor a consistent healed injury across several time periods.

entries.name: Silhouette
entries.definition: The recognizable outer contour of a figure or object when internal detail is reduced or ignored. Appearance silhouette is a shape property; a lighting silhouette is an image in which the subject appears relatively dark.
entries.use: Make characters and objects distinguishable at distance or in brief views. Costume, hair, posture, and carried items all affect the contour.
entries.example: A courier's asymmetric satchel and short cape identify her before the camera reaches her face.

entries.name: Material
entries.definition: The substance an object is made from, or is designed to appear made from, such as wood, wool, glass, or steel. Actual fabrication material and fictional represented material may differ.
entries.use: Connect surfaces to resources, manufacturing, function, and sound. Record substitutions when a lightweight or flexible object must read as another substance.
entries.example: A lightweight scenic panel is finished to resemble heavy cast iron in an abandoned pumping station.

entries.name: Texture
entries.definition: The visual or tactile character of a surface, including roughness, weave, grain, pattern, and small-scale variation. Texture is not identical to material: the same material can receive very different finishes.
entries.use: Add specificity and distinguish objects under the chosen lighting. Test whether fine patterns remain readable and stable at the intended camera distance.
entries.example: The director compares a polished wooden desk with a splintered version to determine which supports the room's history.

entries.name: Patina
entries.definition: A surface character associated with age, exposure, repeated handling, or chemical change, whether naturally acquired or artificially created. Patina can enrich a surface without implying that the object is broken.
entries.use: Suggest a history of environment and care rather than applying uniform dirt everywhere. Place changes where use and exposure plausibly produce them.
entries.example: A brass door handle remains bright where hands touch it but darkens in its recessed ornament.

entries.name: Wear
entries.definition: Deterioration or alteration caused by repeated use, contact, stress, or weathering. Wear includes fraying, scratches, fading, dents, and worn-through areas; it overlaps with patina but emphasizes use and damage.
entries.use: Reveal routines and changing conditions through specific contact points. Track new damage when it becomes a continuity fact.
entries.example: A delivery worker's right coat cuff is more worn because it repeatedly rubs against a bicycle grip.

entries.name: Palette
entries.definition: A selected family of colors and their relationships within an object, character, environment, or production. A palette includes relative prominence and placement, not merely a list of swatches.
entries.use: Coordinate departments and make meaningful departures visible. Separate colors built into costumes and sets from lighting color and later grading adjustments.
entries.example: A muted green workshop contains one orange safety cabinet whose color becomes associated with a concealed document.

entries.name: Shape language
entries.definition: A recurring vocabulary of contours and forms, such as rounded enclosures, narrow verticals, broad wedges, or repeated arches. It is an art-direction description rather than a universal psychological code.
entries.use: Create family resemblance across architecture, props, and costume, or deliberately distinguish competing cultures and organizations.
entries.example: A municipal service uses circular windows, rounded badges, and curved desks, while a private contractor introduces severe rectangular replacements.

entries.name: Scale
entries.definition: Size understood relative to people, neighboring objects, a reference dimension, or a model's represented world. Scale can describe actual construction and apparent size in the image, which need separate records.
entries.use: Shape bodily access, spatial relationships, and perceived institutional importance. Perspective tricks or miniatures may alter apparent scale without corresponding full-size construction.
entries.example: An oversized public counter forces visitors to look upward when asking the seated clerk for help.

entries.name: Density
entries.definition: The concentration of visible objects, detail, or occupied space within an area or frame. Density can be uneven, with a crowded corner beside a deliberately empty surface.
entries.use: Describe accumulation, activity, scarcity of space, or controlled order. Distinguish an overall busy environment from the density actually visible in a chosen shot.
entries.example: A collector's packed shelves stop abruptly around a blank rectangle where one important object was removed.

entries.name: Repetition
entries.definition: The recurrence of a form, object, color, or arrangement within a design. Repetition may be regular or approximate; its pattern can make an exception more noticeable.
entries.use: Suggest production systems, routines, institutional order, or shared ownership. Clarify whether the repeated element is simply practical or carries intended narrative emphasis.
entries.example: Identical numbered lockers line a corridor except for one handmade wooden replacement.

entries.name: Visual hierarchy
entries.definition: The relative prominence of visible elements and the order in which a composition encourages attention. Size, contrast, placement, grouping, detail, and illumination can contribute together.
entries.use: Support the intended reading of a set or character without assuming that every viewer will look in the same order. Check hierarchy through the actual lens and frame.
entries.example: A bright white envelope on a nearly empty dark desk becomes easier to notice than the richly decorated walls.

entries.name: Period authenticity
entries.definition: The extent to which design choices are supported by evidence about a specified historical time, place, community, and use. It is contextual accuracy, not simply the presence of old-looking objects.
entries.use: Ground decisions in documented construction, clothing, availability, and habits. Identify deliberate exceptions and gaps in evidence instead of presenting guesses as verified facts.
entries.example: A shop interior uses researched regional packaging while marking an invented brand as a fictional substitution.

entries.name: Stylization
entries.definition: Deliberate selection, simplification, exaggeration, or transformation of visible reality according to a formal design approach. Stylization can coexist with accurate historical research and functional objects.
entries.use: Create a coherent visual world by deciding which qualities to amplify and which to omit. State the rule concretely rather than calling everything “cinematic.”
entries.example: A period train station retains plausible construction but simplifies all advertising to two colors and unusually large lettering.

entries.name: Lived-in detail
entries.definition: Specific evidence that a space or object has been used by particular people over time. It includes organization, repairs, adaptations, and omissions, rather than being synonymous with mess.
entries.use: Tie decoration to routines and biography. A carefully maintained room can feel inhabited when its arrangements reveal consistent purposes.
entries.example: A kettle handle has a cloth wrap, and the nearest cupboard contains matching replacement strips cut to size.

entries.name: Visual continuity
entries.definition: Consistency, or deliberately tracked change, in visible details across shots and story time. It includes placement, condition, costume, hair, makeup, and the progressive effects of action.
entries.use: Let scenes shot separately describe a coherent event. Continuity records should follow fictional chronology as well as production order.
entries.example: A coat acquires a torn pocket during a chase, and every subsequent scene preserves that damage until a repair occurs.

entries.name: Extreme wide shot
entries.definition: A framing in which the environment occupies most of the image and the principal subject, if visible, appears very small. Also called an extreme long shot or EWS/ELS.
entries.use: Establish large spatial relationships, show collective activity, or relate an individual to an extensive setting. It need not be the first shot of a scene.
entries.example: A single maintenance worker crosses the illuminated floor of an otherwise dark aircraft hangar.

entries.name: Wide shot
entries.definition: A relatively expansive framing that presents the subject together with substantial surroundings. Often called a long shot or WS/LS, although usage overlaps with full shot and differs among crews.
entries.use: Make geography, body movement, and relationships readable within one image. Specify the necessary boundaries when the label alone is ambiguous.
entries.example: The frame includes a shopkeeper, the customer at the counter, and the open back door between them.

entries.name: Full shot
entries.definition: A framing that includes a person's whole body from head to feet, usually with less environmental emphasis than a wide shot. Full-length shot is a common alternative name.
entries.use: Preserve posture, gesture, costume silhouette, and footwork. A full shot describes body coverage rather than a fixed lens choice or camera distance.
entries.example: A dancer pauses in a doorway, with both the hesitant hand movement and planted feet visible.

entries.name: Medium long shot
entries.definition: A framing commonly extending from around the knees to above the head. MLS is a frequent abbreviation; “three-quarter shot” overlaps, while a cowboy shot often specifies approximately mid-thigh framing.
entries.use: Keep substantial bodily action while making expressions easier to read than in a full shot. Confirm the intended crop rather than assuming exact agreement.
entries.example: A station guard's face, radio hand, and shifting stance remain visible during a disputed entry.

entries.name: Medium shot
entries.definition: A framing commonly showing a person from roughly the waist upward. MS is the usual abbreviation; the boundary is a practical convention rather than a measurement standard.
entries.use: Balance facial expression with hand gestures and nearby action. A medium shot can include multiple people if their scale within the frame is comparable.
entries.example: A baker folds a paper bag while answering a customer's unexpectedly personal question.

entries.name: Medium close-up
entries.definition: A framing commonly extending from the upper chest or shoulders to above the head. MCU sits between a medium shot and a close-up, with terminology varying slightly across productions.
entries.use: Emphasize facial response while retaining some posture and environmental context. Check how the chosen aspect ratio changes space around the subject.
entries.example: A teacher reads a note, and the small movement of her shoulders remains visible as she understands it.

entries.name: Close-up
entries.definition: A framing in which a face or another selected subject occupies much of the image. CU describes relative image scale; a close-up of an object does not require human-body landmarks.
entries.use: Make a detail or response available for sustained scrutiny. A close-up can clarify information, withhold surroundings, or create emphasis without necessarily indicating intimacy.
entries.example: The camera holds on a locksmith's face as he recognizes the mechanism's unusual sound.

entries.name: Extreme close-up
entries.definition: A very tight framing of a small portion of a subject, such as an eye, a fingertip, or part of a mechanism. ECU and detail shot are common related labels.
entries.use: Isolate information whose significance might be lost in a broader image. Orientation may need support from neighboring shots.
entries.example: The image shows the instant a fine crack spreads through the glass of a pressure gauge.

entries.name: Eye level
entries.definition: A viewpoint positioned approximately at the subject's eye height, commonly with a relatively level viewing direction. Camera height and tilt should still be specified separately when precision matters.
entries.use: Establish a direct spatial relationship without a pronounced view from above or below. Eye level does not guarantee neutrality or equal social power.
entries.example: The camera is lowered to a seated child's eyes while an adult waits outside the frame.

entries.name: High angle
entries.definition: A viewpoint looking downward toward the subject. The amount of downward inclination and the camera's distance both affect the resulting view; high angle does not necessarily mean directly overhead.
entries.use: Expose floor relationships, show activity behind a foreground subject, or describe an elevated observer's position. Emotional interpretations depend on context.
entries.example: From a stair landing, the frame reveals where each guest has placed their wet shoes around the entrance.

entries.name: Low angle
entries.definition: A viewpoint looking upward toward the subject. It can arise from a low camera position, a raised subject, or both, and varies from subtle inclination to a steep upward view.
entries.use: Reveal ceilings, connect figures to architecture, or adopt a lower observer's vantage. It does not inherently make a subject powerful.
entries.example: A technician peers upward through floor machinery as a colleague lowers a missing component toward her.

entries.name: Overhead
entries.definition: A viewpoint looking approximately straight down onto the action. Also called a top shot or bird's-eye view, though “bird's-eye” sometimes describes a less strictly vertical elevated view.
entries.use: Present spatial patterns, simultaneous tasks, or relationships difficult to see from the side. Height alone does not make a shot overhead; viewing direction matters.
entries.example: An overhead image reveals two hands moving toward the same unclaimed envelope across a round table.

entries.name: Canted angle
entries.definition: A framing rotated around the camera's viewing axis so normally level or vertical references appear tilted. Dutch angle or Dutch tilt are common aliases; it differs from tilting the camera upward or downward.
entries.use: Establish a graphic imbalance or a particular viewpoint. Disorientation is one possible contextual effect, not an automatic meaning.
entries.example: A camera aligned with a ship's listing deck makes the shore beyond appear sharply diagonal.

entries.name: Single
entries.definition: A shot organized primarily around one person. A clean single excludes another participant's foreground body; a dirty single includes part of another person or an intervening element.
entries.use: Give an individual response or action its own emphasis while retaining flexibility about environmental context. “Single” does not specify shot size.
entries.example: During a council vote, each member receives a medium single before the group result is shown.

entries.name: Two-shot
entries.definition: A shot organized around two people together. Their relative sizes, orientations, and depth positions can differ; they do not need to stand side by side or face the camera.
entries.use: Let a relationship unfold within one continuous image and show simultaneous responses. Specify whether one person dominates the framing.
entries.example: A father sits in the foreground while his adult daughter remains standing in the open doorway behind him.

entries.name: Group shot
entries.definition: A shot organized around several people as a shared arrangement. The group can contain internal clusters or unequal prominence; it is more than a count of incidental background figures.
entries.use: Show alliances, collective reactions, or competing actions without separating everyone into singles. Blocking and depth become important tools for readability.
entries.example: A band hears its first recorded performance together, with each member responding differently in the same frame.

entries.name: Over-the-shoulder shot
entries.definition: A view past part of a foreground person's shoulder, head, or upper body toward another subject. OTS is the common abbreviation; it establishes a spatial relationship rather than literal first-person vision.
entries.use: Connect participants while emphasizing the person or object beyond. Foreground size and focus affect how strongly the nearer person occupies the exchange.
entries.example: The blurred shoulder of a customer frames the clerk quietly sliding a returned photograph across the counter.

entries.name: Establishing shot
entries.definition: A shot that supplies useful context about location, geography, time, or relationships for an upcoming or ongoing passage. It is a function, not necessarily a wide exterior view.
entries.use: Give viewers enough orientation to interpret later details. Establishing information may be distributed across several shots or deliberately postponed.
entries.example: A close view of an operating-room clock and illuminated status sign establishes a night surgery before faces appear.

entries.name: Master shot
entries.definition: A shot that covers the main action of a scene through a substantial continuous span, commonly including its principal participants. It provides a broad account that may be combined with closer coverage.
entries.use: Preserve performance relationships and an editorial foundation. A master need not remain wide or static, and an establishing shot need not cover complete action.
entries.example: One moving take follows the entire argument from the apartment entrance to the kitchen table.

entries.name: Insert
entries.definition: A shot emphasizing a detail within the scene's action or immediate space, often an object or small gesture. Its scale is frequently close, but its informational relationship is what matters.
entries.use: Clarify an action, expose evidence, or make a detail available at the necessary moment. Coordinate object state and hand positions with surrounding coverage.
entries.example: Between conversation shots, an insert reveals the date printed on the visitor's expired access card.

entries.name: Cutaway
entries.definition: A shot that shifts attention away from the principal action to something related, nearby, or contextually relevant. Compared with an insert, it more clearly leaves the main action's immediate detail.
entries.use: Broaden context, introduce another response, or bridge an editorial omission. The boundary between insert and cutaway varies by usage.
entries.example: During a platform farewell, the film cuts away to the departure board changing from delayed to boarding.

entries.name: Reaction shot
entries.definition: A shot whose primary function is to show a response to another event, action, or piece of information. It can show a face, a whole body, or a group.
entries.use: Establish what an event means to a participant and determine whose response guides interpretation. A reaction can precede the audience's view of its cause.
entries.example: The editor shows the assistant's startled look before revealing the empty display case.

entries.name: Point-of-view shot
entries.definition: A shot presented as what a particular character sees from their position. POV is the common abbreviation; its identification usually relies on surrounding shots, gaze, sound, or established context.
entries.use: Restrict visual access to a character's viewpoint or make looking itself significant. An over-the-shoulder shot is not automatically a literal POV.
entries.example: After a child raises binoculars, the next image shows the distant ferry through the binocular view.

entries.name: Symmetry
entries.definition: An arrangement in which visual elements correspond across an axis or around a center. Symmetry can be exact, approximate, or temporarily disrupted as people and camera positions change.
entries.use: Establish a legible pattern whose stability or interruption matters. Symmetry may support formality, humor, or discomfort depending on the scene.
entries.example: Two identical waiting-room benches balance the frame until one applicant stands and leaves an empty half.

entries.name: Asymmetry
entries.definition: An arrangement without matching distribution across the frame's principal axes. Asymmetry can still feel balanced through differences in size, contrast, depth, or the implied weight of attention.
entries.use: Hold competing points of interest or reserve meaningful space. It is a compositional description, not a synonym for carelessness or instability.
entries.example: A small bright exit sign on one side counterbalances a large dark figure on the other.

entries.name: Central framing
entries.definition: Placement of the principal subject near the frame's center. Central framing concerns location; the surrounding image may remain asymmetrical and the subject may face in any direction.
entries.use: Sustain direct attention, preserve space around a moving subject, or work with a setting's geometry. It has no mandatory emotional effect.
entries.example: A courier stays centered while commuters stream unevenly past on both sides.

entries.name: Rule of thirds
entries.definition: A compositional guide that divides the frame into three equal horizontal and vertical bands, suggesting lines and intersections as possible placements for important elements. It is a heuristic, not a rule of correctness.
entries.use: Compare arrangements and discuss displacement from the center. Other proportions may serve the scene equally well.
entries.example: A horizon rests near the lower third so the changing cloud cover dominates the landscape.

entries.name: Negative space
entries.definition: Areas around or between principal subjects that contain relatively little competing visual information. Negative space may be textured, dark, bright, or environmentally detailed while remaining subordinate to the subject.
entries.use: Shape isolation, direction, anticipation, or graphic balance through a contextual relationship. Its meaning changes when another subject enters it.
entries.example: An interview frame leaves an empty chair-sized area beside a person discussing someone absent.

entries.name: Headroom
entries.definition: The visible space between the top of a subject's head and the upper frame boundary. It is a framing relationship and can change with movement, aspect ratio, or intended delivery crop.
entries.use: Control vertical placement and compare shots in a sequence. Very tight framing may deliberately crop the head rather than preserve conventional headroom.
entries.example: A character rises from a chair, and the camera reframes to avoid an unintended crop of the eyes.

entries.name: Looking room
entries.definition: Space left in the direction a subject looks. Look room and nose room are common aliases; movement-oriented lead room is related but concerns travel rather than gaze alone.
entries.use: Suggest attention beyond the subject and organize unseen space. Reducing looking room can be deliberate when the frame should feel obstructed or closed.
entries.example: A woman looks toward the right edge, with open space reserved there until her friend enters.

entries.name: Frame within a frame
entries.definition: Use of an element inside the image, such as a doorway, window, mirror, or arch, to enclose or bracket another subject. The internal frame can be partial or complete.
entries.use: Direct attention, connect spaces, or establish a viewpoint through a threshold. An internal frame need not be symmetrical or rectangular.
entries.example: A nurse is visible through the small glazed panel of a door while the corridor remains in the foreground.

entries.name: Leading lines
entries.definition: Visible or implied lines that encourage the eye to move toward, away from, or between elements. Architectural edges, paths, shadows, and aligned objects can all create them.
entries.use: Organize spatial reading and connect points of interest. Lines can also divert attention or terminate in an intentionally empty area.
entries.example: Rows of overhead cables converge toward a lone maintenance platform at the end of a tunnel.

entries.name: Foreground layering
entries.definition: Placement of nearer elements between the camera and principal action to establish overlapping planes. The foreground may be sharp, blurred, moving, or partially occluding the subject.
entries.use: Articulate depth, establish a viewing position, or let information appear through gaps. Too much obstruction may hide action that the audience needs to follow.
entries.example: Hanging laundry intermittently reveals a conversation occurring in the courtyard beyond.

entries.name: Aspect ratio
entries.definition: The proportional relationship of an image's width to its height, commonly expressed as 16:9 or 2.39:1. Delivery ratio, recorded image area, and displayed crop can differ.
entries.use: Plan composition and protect the intended image across versions. ARRI's frame-line tool explicitly distinguishes camera formats and target ratios. [ARRI, Frame Line & Lens Illumination Tool](https://www.arri.com/en/learn-help/learn-help-camera-system/tools/frame-line-lens-illumination-tool).
entries.example: A production records extra image area while composing a primary 1.85:1 presentation.

entries.name: Portrait frame
entries.definition: A frame taller than it is wide, with a width-to-height ratio below one. Vertical frame is an ordinary alias; 9:16 is one possible ratio rather than the definition.
entries.use: Organize vertical relationships, full figures, or work intended for vertical display. Reconsider blocking and background information when adapting a wider composition.
entries.example: A lift shaft fills a vertical frame, relating a mechanic at its base to a stranded passenger above.

entries.name: Widescreen frame
entries.definition: A broad horizontal frame, conventionally wider than the older roughly 4:3 screen shape. The term covers multiple ratios, so “widescreen” alone is not a complete delivery specification.
entries.use: Explore lateral relationships, landscape, or simultaneous action. It does not dictate shot size, genre, lens type, or the amount of visible background.
entries.example: Two estranged friends occupy opposite ends of a wide image while a closed ticket window separates them.

entries.name: Split screen
entries.definition: Presentation of two or more distinct images within the same overall frame. Panels may show simultaneous events, different times, contrasting views, or a graphic arrangement unrelated to ordinary chronology.
entries.use: Compare actions and information while deciding how attention should move between panels. Synchronization needs to be specified rather than inferred from proximity.
entries.example: One panel shows a caller waiting silently while another shows the recipient deciding whether to answer.

entries.name: Pan
entries.definition: Rotation of the camera left or right about a generally vertical axis. The camera's orientation changes; a pure pan does not translate the viewpoint sideways through the scene.
entries.use: Follow lateral action, compare adjacent areas, or reveal something outside the initial frame. A pan can be combined with translation and other rotations.
entries.example: From one tripod position, the camera pans from a departing bus to the passenger left behind.

entries.name: Tilt
entries.definition: Rotation of the camera upward or downward about a generally horizontal axis. Tilting changes viewing direction, whereas raising or lowering the whole camera changes its position.
entries.use: Follow vertical attention, describe height, or connect details at different elevations. Specify whether the support also moves during the shot.
entries.example: The camera tilts from a child's muddy boots to the immaculate portrait she is carrying overhead.

entries.name: Roll
entries.definition: Rotation around the camera's viewing axis, making the image turn clockwise or counterclockwise. Roll changes the horizon's orientation without necessarily changing where the center of the frame points.
entries.use: Describe physical rotation, an unusual viewpoint, or a deliberate graphic transition. A fixed rolled position produces a canted framing.
entries.example: As a mechanic turns inside a circular access tunnel, the camera rolls to maintain alignment with her body.

entries.name: Dolly in
entries.definition: Physical camera movement toward a subject or chosen scene point. Push-in is a common alias. The name often describes the movement even when a wheeled dolly is not the support.
entries.use: Change viewpoint and progressively alter a subject's prominence or surrounding relationships. It differs optically from changing focal length at a fixed position.
entries.example: The camera advances toward a seated witness as she notices a familiar mark on the evidence bag.

entries.name: Dolly out
entries.definition: Physical camera movement away from a subject or chosen scene point. Pull-back or pull-out are common aliases, although local terminology should be confirmed when another support is used.
entries.use: Reveal surrounding space, redistribute attention, or change the audience's spatial relation to an action. A backward move can also maintain framing on an approaching subject.
entries.example: The camera withdraws from a carefully set table until the empty warehouse around it becomes visible.

entries.name: Lateral tracking
entries.definition: Camera translation sideways relative to a defined scene axis or subject relationship. Trucking and side tracking are common related names; the camera can aim straight ahead or rotate while traveling.
entries.use: Follow parallel action, compare adjacent spaces, or create depth changes through parallax. Identify the reference direction because “left” can mean screen-left or world-left.
entries.example: The camera travels beside a row of train windows, revealing different passengers in successive compartments.

entries.name: Pedestal up
entries.definition: Raising the camera vertically while its viewing direction may remain fixed. Pedestal describes position change, not the upward rotation of a tilt; boom up is sometimes used for related support motion.
entries.use: See over an obstruction or change the relationship between foreground and background. Confirm whether the actual support produces a vertical line or a slight arc.
entries.example: The camera rises above stacked crates to reveal a person hiding behind them.

entries.name: Pedestal down
entries.definition: Lowering the camera vertically, independently of whether it also changes orientation. It differs from tilting down because the viewpoint itself descends through space.
entries.use: Move from one height relationship to another, pass beneath an obstruction, or meet a seated subject's level. Record any simultaneous tilt separately.
entries.example: As an adult kneels to speak to a child, the camera descends and keeps both faces at a similar image height.

entries.name: Crane movement
entries.definition: Camera travel produced by a crane or jib, potentially combining elevation, lateral reach, and sweeping arcs. A crane is a support mechanism, so its movement still requires a described path.
entries.use: Connect levels or reveal geography beyond ordinary standing camera positions. Different crane designs allow different trajectories; the label alone does not specify the result.
entries.example: A shot begins beside a ticket queue and rises over the booth to reveal the empty stadium beyond.

entries.name: Orbit
entries.definition: A path traveling around a subject or selected center, commonly while keeping the camera aimed toward it. An orbit may cover part of a circle or continue through a full revolution.
entries.use: Reveal changing background relationships while retaining a central subject. State radius, angular coverage, and orientation behavior where useful.
entries.example: The camera circles a stalled car until the hidden damage on its far side becomes visible.

entries.name: Arc
entries.definition: A curved segment of camera travel. An arc may bend around a subject, but it does not require constant radius, a fixed center, or continuous inward-facing orientation.
entries.use: Move between viewpoints smoothly while controlling what passes in front of the lens. “Arc” and “orbit” overlap in everyday shot descriptions.
entries.example: The camera curves from behind a receptionist to a three-quarter view of the visitor approaching the desk.

entries.name: Follow
entries.definition: Camera movement that accompanies a subject, commonly from behind or beside them. It describes the camera-subject relationship rather than a particular support, lens, or path shape.
entries.use: Let movement through an environment structure the audience's discovery. Decide how closely the camera maintains distance and how independently it looks around.
entries.example: The camera follows a night porter through service corridors, discovering each locked door when he reaches it.

entries.name: Lead
entries.definition: Camera movement ahead of a moving subject, commonly traveling backward while looking toward them. Lead describes relative placement and accompaniment; it does not prescribe how the camera is supported.
entries.use: Preserve access to a moving performer's face while allowing the environment to unfold behind. The path and subject distance need coordination.
entries.example: The camera retreats ahead of two sisters as they walk toward an appointment neither wants to discuss.

entries.name: Locked-off camera
entries.definition: A camera held at a fixed position and orientation for the intended duration of a shot. Lens focus or focal length could still change, so “locked-off” does not automatically freeze every image property.
entries.use: Let action enter, leave, and reorganize a stable frame, or support aligned repeated takes. Specify any permitted lens adjustments.
entries.example: One fixed view records a café opening, filling with customers, and emptying after an unexpected announcement.

entries.name: Handheld camera
entries.definition: A camera substantially carried and guided by the operator's hands and body, without a support intended to isolate all bodily movement. Handheld operation can range from restrained to visibly unsettled.
entries.use: Respond flexibly to performers or accommodate constrained spaces. Handheld texture does not by itself prove documentary authenticity or create urgency.
entries.example: An operator adjusts position among cooks working in a narrow kitchen during a single busy service.

entries.name: Shoulder rig
entries.definition: A support configuration resting part of a camera's weight on the operator's shoulder, often with handles and other contact points. It changes handling and load distribution without eliminating bodily movement.
entries.use: Sustain mobile operating with a particular camera height and physical response. Shoulder-mounted operation remains compatible with handheld aesthetics and varied movement paths.
entries.example: A shoulder-mounted camera accompanies a supervisor inspecting a production line while the operator makes small reframing adjustments.

entries.name: Stabilized camera
entries.definition: A camera whose unwanted movement is reduced by a stabilization system or process. Stabilization may be mechanical, electronic, optical, sensor-based, or applied in post-production; these produce different constraints and artifacts.
entries.use: Specify the desired motion character independently from the system used. Stabilization does not mean the camera cannot intentionally move or shake.
entries.example: A walking shot maintains a relatively steady horizon while still advancing through a crowded entrance hall.

entries.name: Gimbal
entries.definition: A pivoted support allowing rotation around one or more axes. In contemporary production shorthand, it often means a motorized stabilizer that controls camera orientation; not every gimbal is electronic.
entries.use: Separate some unwanted angular movement from intentional aiming. Translational bobbing, operating skill, balance, and payload still affect the result.
entries.example: A motorized three-axis gimbal keeps the camera aimed toward a courier while the operator walks an adjacent path.

entries.name: Steadicam
entries.definition: A trademarked family of camera stabilization systems associated with Tiffen, including body-supported configurations. It is a specific brand, not a generic name for every gimbal or smooth moving shot. [Tiffen, Steadicam](https://tiffen.com/pages/steadicam).
entries.use: Name the intended system when its operating characteristics matter; otherwise describe stabilization and path separately.
entries.example: A Steadicam operator follows a performer from a courtyard through a doorway into a continuous interior scene.

entries.name: Vehicle mount
entries.definition: A support attaching a camera to a vehicle or vehicle-associated rig. The view may face passengers, the vehicle's body, the road, or action traveling alongside.
entries.use: Establish a consistent camera-vehicle relationship while distinguishing it from a camera carried by an occupant. Describe the desired frame separately from the engineered mounting solution.
entries.example: A fixed exterior view keeps the bus driver's reflection aligned with a changing streetscape.

entries.name: Aerial camera
entries.definition: A camera operating from an airborne platform, such as an aircraft or drone. It is a platform description; an elevated crane shot is not automatically an aerial shot.
entries.use: Show large geographical relationships or travel through viewpoints inaccessible from the ground. Specify path, height reference, orientation, and subject relation independently.
entries.example: An aerial view follows a flood channel until it reaches the first houses of a settlement.

entries.name: Motivated movement
entries.definition: Camera movement with an apparent trigger or reason in the unfolding action, attention, or information of the scene. Motivation may be a glance, a sound, a person's movement, or a developing thought.
entries.use: Link camera behavior to what matters at a particular moment. Motivation can be subtle and need not be literal imitation of a character's eyes.
entries.example: A faint knock prompts a slow pan toward a door previously left outside the frame.

entries.name: Unmotivated movement
entries.definition: Movement without an immediately evident trigger in the depicted action or a character's attention. The label describes its relationship to scene events, not an absence of artistic purpose.
entries.use: Explore an independent narrator-like camera, sustained formal pattern, or atmosphere. Record the intended reason even when characters provide no visible cue.
entries.example: The camera drifts away from an ordinary conversation and studies the unused end of the room.

entries.name: Reveal
entries.definition: A movement that makes previously unseen visual information available through a change in framing or viewpoint. The information can have been outside the frame, hidden behind an object, or obscured by an angle.
entries.use: Control when a spatial fact becomes knowable. A reveal is a function, compatible with pans, tracking, rises, and other moves.
entries.example: A lateral move clears a pillar and exposes a second suitcase beside the missing traveler's bag.

entries.name: Reframing
entries.definition: Adjusting the image's boundaries or subject placement during a shot. Reframing may use rotation, translation, focal-length change, or a planned post-production crop, which should be identified separately.
entries.use: Maintain readable action or intentionally shift emphasis as circumstances change. A small correction and a conspicuous compositional change are both forms of reframing.
entries.example: When one person stands, a subtle tilt preserves both her face and the seated listener's response.

entries.name: Whip pan
entries.definition: A very rapid pan, often producing a brief interval of pronounced motion blur. Swish pan is a common alias; the term still describes angular movement rather than lateral translation.
entries.use: Redirect attention abruptly or connect shots through similar blurred movement. Blur amount depends on motion, shutter timing, and scene detail.
entries.example: The camera snaps from a dropped tray to the doorway where everyone suddenly looks.

entries.name: Path
entries.definition: The trajectory followed by the camera's position through space. A path describes where it travels, while orientation describes where it points; either may change independently.
entries.use: Plan spatial reveals and coordinate repeatability with performers and support. A drawn path is schematic unless its coordinate system and measurements are defined.
entries.example: An L-shaped route passes along a shelving aisle before turning into the room behind it.

entries.name: Direction
entries.definition: The orientation of travel or rotation relative to a stated reference, such as world axes, screen space, the camera, or a subject. “Forward” is ambiguous without that reference.
entries.use: Make movement notes interpretable across diagrams, shot lists, and operators. Distinguish clockwise travel around a subject from clockwise camera roll.
entries.example: A note specifies movement toward the doorway in world space while the camera continues looking backward at the speaker.

entries.name: Travel distance
entries.definition: The length covered along a camera's translation path, normally measured in meters or feet. It differs from straight-line displacement between endpoints when the route bends.
entries.use: Relate path geometry to duration, speed, framing, and available space. Pure rotation has angular travel but no intended translational distance.
entries.example: A curved route covers four meters even though its end position is only two meters from its start.

entries.name: Duration
entries.definition: The time occupied by a defined camera movement or interval, normally measured in seconds. Movement duration and final shot duration differ when the shot holds before or after the move.
entries.use: Coordinate a reveal with dialogue, gesture, or editing. Identify whether timing refers to capture time or playback time when footage is retimed.
entries.example: A six-second shot holds for two seconds, moves for three, and settles for one.

entries.name: Speed profile
entries.definition: How travel or rotation speed changes over time. A profile can remain constant, ease in and out, pause, surge, or respond to a moving subject.
entries.use: Describe the feel and timing of a move beyond its total distance and duration. Linear speed and angular speed need different units.
entries.example: A camera begins almost imperceptibly, travels faster across an empty wall, then slows as a hidden portrait enters view.

entries.name: Acceleration
entries.definition: Change in velocity over time, including change of direction as well as speed. Linear acceleration uses units such as meters per second squared; angular acceleration requires an angular measure.
entries.use: Discuss starts, stops, turns, and physically plausible transitions. A constant-speed orbit still changes velocity direction and therefore has acceleration.
entries.example: A programmed move gradually increases from rest so the first shift in viewpoint does not arrive as a visible jolt.

entries.name: Subject tracking
entries.definition: Maintaining a chosen relationship to a subject as it or the camera moves. It may mean following position, keeping the subject framed, or using a tracking system; it does not automatically mean continuous focus.
entries.use: Specify what stays controlled: aim, screen position, distance, or focus. Avoid one checkbox silently promising all four.
entries.example: A pan keeps a cyclist near frame center while focus is adjusted independently as the cyclist approaches.

entries.name: Zoom in
entries.definition: Increasing a zoom lens's focal length during a shot, narrowing the field of view for a fixed active image area. The camera can remain stationary while the subject becomes larger in the frame.
entries.use: Change image scale without the viewpoint change of a dolly move. Lens behavior may introduce additional optical changes.
entries.example: From a fixed observation window, a zoom isolates one numbered crate on the loading dock.

entries.name: Zoom out
entries.definition: Decreasing a zoom lens's focal length during a shot, widening the field of view for a fixed active image area. It reveals additional surrounding image area without requiring backward camera travel.
entries.use: Expand visual context while maintaining approximately the same viewpoint. Distinguish optical zoom from a changing digital crop.
entries.example: A close view of a handwritten sign widens to show that dozens of identical signs fill the room.

entries.name: Dolly zoom
entries.definition: Coordinated camera translation and an opposing focal-length change that keep a chosen subject approximately the same image size while perspective relationships change. Moving away while zooming in is one version. [DJI, introduction to dolly zoom](https://repair.dji.com/help/content?customId=01700006815&documentType=&lang=en&paperDocType=ARTICLE&re=US&spaceId=17).
entries.use: Make changing depth relationships conspicuous; sufficient subject-background separation helps the effect read.
entries.example: The camera retreats from a seated passenger while zooming in, making the platform beyond appear to expand around her.

entries.name: Focal length
entries.definition: An optical property conventionally stated in millimeters, not the physical barrel length. For a fixed active image area, a longer focal length generally yields a narrower field of view. [Nikon, understanding focal length](https://www.nikonusa.com/learn-and-explore/c/tips-and-techniques/understanding-focal-length).
entries.use: Specify lens choice together with format and camera position; focal length alone does not specify perspective or shot size.
entries.example: A 50 mm lens frames different amounts of the same room when the camera switches between full-width and cropped recording modes.

entries.name: Field of view
entries.definition: The extent of the scene captured, expressed as an angular span or a visible width and height at a stated distance. FOV depends on focal length and active image area, with lens projection and focus also relevant.
entries.use: Compare framing consistently by specifying horizontal, vertical, or diagonal angle. Do not present “35 mm” as a complete viewing-angle specification.
entries.example: Two camera modes use the same lens but show different horizontal spans because one crops the sensor.

entries.name: Wide-angle lens
entries.definition: A lens providing a relatively broad angle of view for its capture format, generally with focal length shorter than that format's normal range. “Wide” is therefore format-dependent.
entries.use: Include more surrounding space or work from a nearby viewpoint. Apparent exaggeration of near-far size relationships comes from camera position, not focal length alone.
entries.example: In a cramped lift, a wide lens includes both passengers and the control panel from the available corner.

entries.name: Normal lens
entries.definition: A lens in the conventional middle range for a format, often near the image diagonal in focal length. Standard lens is a common alias; there is no single lens that reproduces the full human visual experience.
entries.use: Establish a reference point between wider and narrower framing options. Confirm format and desired camera distance rather than assuming “normal” means universally neutral.
entries.example: A filmmaker tests a standard-range lens for a conversation where modest environmental context remains useful.

entries.name: Telephoto lens
entries.definition: In common filmmaking usage, a relatively long lens giving a narrow field of view for the format. Strict optical usage also describes a design whose physical length is shorter than its effective focal length.
entries.use: Frame distant details or work from a farther viewpoint. So-called compression reflects camera distance when framing is matched.
entries.example: From across a courtyard, a long lens isolates a person at a window without moving the camera closer.

entries.name: Prime lens
entries.definition: A lens with one nominal focal length rather than an adjustable zoom range. Changing focus may still slightly change framing through focus breathing, so fixed focal length does not promise a perfectly fixed image.
entries.use: Choose a particular optical character and working setup. Primes vary greatly; the label alone guarantees neither superior sharpness nor a larger maximum aperture.
entries.example: A sequence uses a 40 mm prime, with camera position changed deliberately between setups.

entries.name: Zoom lens
entries.definition: A lens offering an adjustable range of focal lengths. It permits reframing between takes or a visible focal-length change during a take; focus retention and aperture behavior depend on the design.
entries.use: Adjust framing without swapping lenses or create a deliberate zoom. Check whether the lens maintains focus while zooming rather than assuming it does.
entries.example: A locked camera gradually changes from 35 mm to 70 mm to isolate a figure across the street.

entries.name: Anamorphic lens
entries.definition: A lens system that scales the image differently along horizontal and vertical axes, typically squeezing horizontal information for capture and requiring corresponding desqueezing for display. Squeeze factor and capture area must be recorded. [Canon, EOS C500 Mark II white paper, anamorphic shooting](https://downloads.canon.com/nw/learn/white-papers/cinema-eos/EOS_C500_MarkII_White_Paper.pdf).
entries.use: Explore its framing and optical character; oval blur or streak flares vary by design.
entries.example: A 2× anamorphic image is monitored desqueezed so performers' proportions appear correct.

entries.name: Aperture
entries.definition: The lens opening controlling the cone of light admitted. F-number relates focal length to entrance-pupil diameter; a smaller f-number means a larger relative opening. Cinema T-stops account for light transmission. [Nikon, understanding aperture](https://www.nikonusa.com/learn-and-explore/c/tips-and-techniques/understanding-maximum-aperture).
entries.use: Balance exposure and depth of field with other settings. Smaller openings can increase depth of field but eventually increase diffraction effects.
entries.example: The crew stops down from f/2.8 to f/4 and compensates the reduced light separately.

entries.name: Depth of field
entries.definition: The range of scene distances judged acceptably sharp around the focus distance. It depends on aperture, focal length, focus distance, and the sharpness criterion, which relates to format and viewing conditions. [Canon, EOS-1Ds manual, basic terminology](https://files.canon-europe.com/files/soft24318/manual/EOS1Ds_CUG_EN.pdf).
entries.use: Plan what must remain legible together. Comparisons must state which conditions stay fixed.
entries.example: A camera test checks whether a foreground letter and its reader remain sufficiently sharp at the chosen aperture.

entries.name: Shallow focus
entries.definition: An image treatment in which only a limited depth range appears acceptably sharp, leaving other distances visibly out of focus. It is the resulting selective-focus condition, not a synonym for close-up.
entries.use: Concentrate detail or withhold background information while considering movement and focus tolerance. Background blur also depends on subject-background separation and magnification.
entries.example: A ring on the table is sharp while the person deciding whether to take it remains blurred behind.

entries.name: Deep focus
entries.definition: An image treatment that keeps substantially separated depth planes acceptably sharp at the same time. It describes a visual result, which may be achieved optically or through combined production techniques.
entries.use: Let foreground and background actions remain simultaneously readable. Deep focus does not mean every distance is perfectly sharp or that audience attention becomes uncontrolled.
