entries.example: A child hides a letter near the lens while adults argue clearly in the far doorway.

entries.name: Rack focus
entries.definition: An intentional shift of focus distance during a shot, commonly transferring sharpness between subjects at different depths. Focus pull is a broader related term that also includes maintaining focus on a moving subject.
entries.use: Change which information is optically available without necessarily moving or cutting the camera. Lens breathing may change framing during the adjustment.
entries.example: Focus leaves the listener's face and settles on the visitor reflected in the mirror behind her.

entries.name: Focus distance
entries.definition: The distance from the camera's sensor or film plane to the plane of best focus for an ordinary flat-field setup. It is normally expressed in meters or feet and differs from distance measured from the lens front.
entries.use: Coordinate focus marks, moving subjects, and depth-of-field estimates. Confirm equipment conventions when close distances or unusual optics matter.
entries.example: A focus mark identifies the actor's final position two meters from the sensor-plane reference.

entries.name: Exposure
entries.definition: The light delivered to the recording surface over the exposure interval, and by extension the resulting brightness placement. Illumination, aperture, exposure time, and filtration affect collected light; digital ISO does not itself add photons.
entries.use: Protect the information needed for the intended image while coordinating motion blur and depth of field. Brightness in the final grade is a separate adjustment.
entries.example: Neutral-density filtration reduces incoming light while preserving the chosen aperture and shutter timing.

entries.name: Frame rate
entries.definition: A count of images per second, expressed in fps. Capture frame rate describes acquisition; playback or project frame rate describes presentation. Matching or differing rates produce different timing outcomes.
entries.use: Specify both values when motion speed matters. A high capture rate does not automatically create slow playback. [Sony, slow and quick motion](https://www.sony.com/electronics/support/articles/00286854).
entries.example: A clip captured at 48 fps plays in real time at 48 fps or half speed when conformed frame-for-frame to 24 fps.

entries.name: Shutter angle
entries.definition: Exposure duration expressed as a fraction of a frame cycle using degrees. Under ordinary constant-rate operation, exposure time in seconds equals `shutter_angle_deg / (360 × capture_fps)`. [ARRI, electronic and mirror shutter white paper](https://www.arri.com/resource/blob/186770/ad23969317dafff402f0902d47bb4ab7/alexa-studio-electronic-and-mirror-shutter-white-paper-data.pdf).
entries.use: Relate exposure time to capture rate and motion rendition. It is not a rotation of the camera.
entries.example: At 24 fps, a 180° shutter exposes each frame for approximately 1/48 second.

entries.name: Motion blur
entries.definition: Image smearing produced when scene detail moves across the recording surface during an exposure. It depends on exposure duration, relative motion, magnification, and direction, not merely on playback frame rate.
entries.use: Shape motion rendition while retaining necessary detail. Shorter exposure intervals generally reduce blur for the same motion. [ARRI, shutter white paper](https://www.arri.com/resource/blob/186770/ad23969317dafff402f0902d47bb4ab7/alexa-studio-electronic-and-mirror-shutter-white-paper-data.pdf).
entries.example: A spinning wheel produces longer streaks when the exposure interval increases at the same capture rate.

entries.name: Slow motion
entries.definition: Presentation in which an event occupies more screen time than its original duration. Capturing more frames per second than are played frame-for-frame is one method; post-production interpolation or duplication are others.
entries.use: Reveal brief actions or reshape temporal emphasis. Preserve capture and playback rates so the intended speed can be reproduced. [Sony, high-frame-rate shooting](https://helpguide.sony.net/dsc/1630/v1/en/contents/TP0000829893.html).
entries.example: One second captured at 120 fps becomes five seconds when all frames play at 24 fps.

entries.name: Time-lapse
entries.definition: A sequence captured at widely spaced intervals and presented faster, making a long process unfold in a shorter viewing time. Capture interval and exposure duration are separate quantities.
entries.use: Reveal gradual change, such as construction or shifting weather. Plan the desired screen duration from the number of captured images and playback rate.
entries.example: Recording one frame every ten seconds for an hour yields 360 frames, or fifteen seconds at 24 fps.

entries.name: Sensor or film format
entries.definition: The recording medium's size and configuration, especially the active image area used for a shot. A named format, film gauge, or sensor model may allow multiple recording gates, crops, and aspect ratios.
entries.use: Interpret lens coverage and field of view using active dimensions, not resolution alone. ARRI distinguishes sensor, recording format, and target frame. [ARRI, frame-line tool](https://www.arri.com/en/learn-help/learn-help-camera-system/tools/frame-line-lens-illumination-tool).
entries.example: A camera's cropped high-speed mode changes framing even though the mounted lens remains the same.

entries.name: Grain
entries.definition: The visible granular texture associated with photographic film's image structure, or a deliberately added simulation of it. Apparent grain varies with stock, exposure, processing, enlargement, scanning, and scene content. [Kodak, VISION3 250D technical information](https://www.kodak.com/content/products-brochures/motion-picture/KODAK-VISION3-250D-5207-7207-technical-information.pdf).
entries.use: Discuss texture separately from sharpness and compression artifacts. Record whether grain originated in capture or was added later.
entries.example: A digital sequence receives a tested grain treatment matched across bright walls and darker clothing.

entries.name: Digital noise
entries.definition: Unwanted variation in recorded pixel values arising from photon statistics, sensor electronics, and processing. It may appear as luminance variation, colored speckles, or patterns; it is not the same physical process as film grain.
entries.use: Assess exposure and processing through representative footage. Low signal and shadow lifting can make noise more visible. [ARRI, dynamic-range white paper](https://www.arri.com/resource/blob/295460/e10ff8a5b3abf26c33f8754379b57442/2022-09-28-arri-dynamic-range-whitepaper-data.pdf).
entries.example: A dim corridor test reveals colored fluctuations in the shadows when the image is brightened for the intended grade.

entries.name: Lens distortion
entries.definition: Optical deviation from the intended geometric mapping, commonly visible as barrel, pincushion, or more complex bending of straight lines in a rectilinear image. It differs from viewpoint-dependent perspective. [Canon, correcting distortion](https://global.canon/en/c-museum/special/exhibition1.html).
entries.use: Evaluate architecture, faces near frame edges, and matching across lenses. Correction may alter framing and require cropping.
entries.example: A grid filmed during a lens test reveals that straight door frames bow outward near the image edges.

entries.name: Diffusion
entries.definition: In lens and capture discussion, optical filtration that redistributes some light to alter fine detail, highlight glow, or contrast. Effects vary substantially among filters; diffusion does not necessarily mean deliberate defocus. [Tiffen, diffusion guide](https://tiffen.com/pages/diffusion-guide).
entries.use: Test the intended image character under actual highlights, lens settings, and subject distances. Lighting diffusion is a different intervention.
entries.example: A filter gently spreads bright practical lamps while the actor's eye remains accurately focused.

entries.name: Flare
entries.definition: Unwanted or deliberately welcomed light spread, reflection, or scattering within an optical system, producing veiling brightness, ghosts, streaks, or other artifacts. A bright source can cause flare from within or outside the frame.
entries.use: Consider flare as part of lens character while monitoring contrast and essential detail. Its appearance depends on lens, coating, filtration, angle, and light level.
entries.example: As a car turns, a streetlamp briefly creates a translucent reflection across the windshield view.

entries.name: Key light
entries.definition: The principal source or contribution shaping illumination on a selected subject. It establishes a dominant lighting relationship rather than necessarily being the brightest visible object or a particular fixture type. [ARRI lighting handbook, key light](https://www.arri.com/resource/blob/83996/409091c612f371b0c68b41d9dcb636db/arri-lighting-handbook-english-data.pdf).
entries.use: Identify the main direction and modeling of the subject while coordinating secondary sources.
entries.example: A broad window provides the key on a seated reader, although a small visible lamp is brighter within the image.

entries.name: Fill light
entries.definition: Illumination that raises areas left relatively dark by the key or other dominant source. Fill can come from another fixture, reflected light, or the environment. [ARRI lighting handbook, fill light](https://www.arri.com/resource/blob/83996/409091c612f371b0c68b41d9dcb636db/arri-lighting-handbook-english-data.pdf).
entries.use: Control shadow visibility and the contrast relationship without assuming that every shadow must disappear.
entries.example: A white wall returns enough window light to keep the reader's shaded eye visible.

entries.name: Backlight
entries.definition: Light reaching a subject from behind relative to the camera's view. It may illuminate hair, shoulders, translucent material, or an edge, depending on source position and the subject's shape.
entries.use: Separate layers, reveal transmission through materials, or establish a source behind the action. A backlight is not the same as a light aimed at the background.
entries.example: An open doorway behind a cyclist lights the edge of a wet coat.

entries.name: Rim light
entries.definition: Illumination producing a visible band or edge highlight along a subject's contour. Rim describes the resulting appearance; back or rear-side placement often produces it, but the entire back need not be lit.
entries.use: Make a boundary readable against a similar-toned background. The width and strength of the rim depend on geometry, source size, and material.
entries.example: A narrow highlight outlines a dark instrument case against the backstage curtains.

entries.name: Background light
entries.definition: Illumination directed primarily at the environment behind the main subject. It describes the target of the light, not the source's location behind the subject.
entries.use: Reveal setting, create separation, or organize attention through patches and gradients. Background lighting may coordinate with the apparent direction of a window or practical fixture.
entries.example: A soft pool of light on a noticeboard makes its presence readable while the speaker remains separately lit.

entries.name: Hard light
entries.definition: Light that produces relatively distinct shadow edges, commonly from a source with small apparent size as seen by the subject. Hardness is not the same property as brightness or contrast. [ARRI lighting handbook, light quality](https://www.arri.com/resource/blob/83996/409091c612f371b0c68b41d9dcb636db/arri-lighting-handbook-english-data.pdf).
entries.use: Make shape, cast shadows, or surface relief clear when appropriate to the scene.
entries.example: A small directional source projects the pattern of a railing sharply across the floor.

entries.name: Soft light
entries.definition: Light producing broader, more gradual shadow transitions, commonly from a source with larger apparent size as seen by the subject. A physically large source becomes relatively smaller when moved farther away. [ARRI lighting handbook, light quality](https://www.arri.com/resource/blob/83996/409091c612f371b0c68b41d9dcb636db/arri-lighting-handbook-english-data.pdf).
entries.use: Control shadow transitions without assuming that soft light must be flat or low-contrast.
entries.example: A large nearby luminous surface creates a gradual transition across a sculptor's face.

entries.name: Diffused light
entries.definition: Light transmitted through a scattering material that alters its distribution. When the illuminated material becomes a sufficiently large apparent source, shadows soften; a tiny diffuser does not automatically create very soft light.
entries.use: Change an existing source's delivery while managing its effective size, position, light loss, and spill. “Diffused” names a method, not a guarantee of identical results.
entries.example: A curtain spreads incoming window light into a larger luminous area.

entries.name: Bounced light
entries.definition: Light reflected from a surface before reaching the subject. The bounce surface's size, color, texture, and reflectivity help determine the illumination's quality and color.
entries.use: Redirect light or turn a surface into an effective source. Bounced light is often soft, but a mirror or small reflective area can preserve a hard character.
entries.example: A lamp aimed into a pale ceiling creates a broad return of light over a kitchen table.

entries.name: Frontal
entries.group: Direction relative to the subject and camera
entries.definition: Illumination arriving from roughly the camera-facing side of a subject. Frontal light is a direction, not a statement about hardness, intensity, or whether shadows are completely absent.
entries.use: Preserve visibility on surfaces facing the lens or establish a source near the viewer's position. Specify elevation when facial modeling matters.
entries.example: A ticket examiner's handheld lamp illuminates a passenger from near the camera's line of sight.

entries.name: Side
entries.group: Direction relative to the subject and camera
entries.definition: Illumination arriving predominantly from one side of a subject relative to the camera. Side light can range from a modest off-axis position to a nearly perpendicular direction.
entries.use: Describe volume, surface relief, or distinct illuminated and shaded regions. Its effect depends on the subject's orientation and accompanying fill.
entries.example: Light from a corridor opening crosses a repair worker's hands and exposes the raised lettering on a metal plate.

entries.name: Back
entries.group: Direction relative to the subject and camera
entries.definition: A directional relationship in which light travels toward the camera-facing scene from behind the subject. This names source direction; “backlight” identifies a light or contribution used in that position.
entries.use: Specify a geometry that may create rim highlights, translucency, flare, or silhouette depending on exposure and other illumination.
entries.example: The low sun behind hanging fabric makes its thinner and thicker sections visibly different.

entries.name: Top
entries.group: Direction relative to the subject and camera
entries.definition: Illumination arriving predominantly from above a subject. Top light may be close to vertical or include a forward or sideways component, so height and aim remain useful details.
entries.use: Relate lighting to overhead fixtures, open sky, or a chosen pattern of shadow. It need not imply interrogation, danger, or harshness.
entries.example: An overhead work lamp lights a map while leaving the seated surveyors' lower faces less illuminated.

entries.name: Underlighting
entries.group: Direction relative to the subject and camera
entries.definition: Illumination arriving from below a subject's usual eye or object level. Uplighting is a related name; the source may be visible, concealed, or reflected upward from another surface.
entries.use: Establish plausible low sources or deliberately change familiar shadow patterns. Its meaning depends on the scene and need not be threatening.
entries.example: Reflected pool light moves across the underside of a lifeguard's face during a quiet inspection.

entries.name: High-key lighting
entries.definition: An approach generally characterized by a bright overall tonal range and relatively limited deep shadow, often with substantial fill. It is not simply overexposure or the use of a powerful key light.
entries.use: Keep multiple parts of the image readily visible while controlling important contrast. High-key images can support discomfort or severity as readily as cheerfulness.
entries.example: A nearly white examination room leaves a patient few visually sheltered areas within the frame.

entries.name: Low-key lighting
entries.definition: An approach with substantial dark areas and selective illumination, often producing pronounced light-dark relationships. Low-key lighting does not require accidental underexposure or the loss of every shadow detail.
entries.use: Limit what is visible and concentrate emphasis while preserving the information intended for the grade. A dark image can remain carefully exposed.
entries.example: Only the workbench and a narrow doorway receive light in an otherwise dim instrument workshop.

entries.name: Silhouette
entries.definition: A subject rendered relatively dark against a brighter surrounding region so its outer contour dominates and internal detail is reduced. The result depends on lighting relationships and exposure together.
entries.use: Prioritize recognizable outline, movement, or anonymity. This lighting use differs from discussing a costume's silhouette under ordinary illumination.
entries.example: Two people greeting each other inside a station become dark shapes against the bright platform beyond.

entries.name: Motivated lighting
entries.definition: Lighting designed to appear plausibly caused by an identifiable or implied source within the story's environment. The actual production fixtures can be concealed, supplemented, or positioned differently to achieve that appearance.
entries.use: Connect illumination to the fictional world without requiring the visible source to supply all usable light.
entries.example: A desk lamp motivates a warm pool on an actor's face while a concealed fixture supplies most of that illumination.

entries.name: Available light
entries.definition: Illumination already present at the location, such as daylight, street lighting, or existing interior fixtures. It is not limited to sunlight and does not guarantee that the crew leaves it unmodified.
entries.use: Work with the location's existing conditions, possibly shaping them through scheduling, blocking, reflectors, or subtraction. Record added sources separately.
entries.example: A conversation is staged beside an existing shop window while a dark cloth reduces unwanted reflection from one side.

entries.name: Practical lighting
entries.definition: Use of functioning light sources belonging visibly to the set or story environment, such as table lamps, signs, or lanterns. Practicals may illuminate subjects, motivate additional light, or mainly appear as luminous objects.
entries.use: Coordinate art direction, actor interaction, and lighting control. A practical is not automatically the dominant source.
entries.example: A character switches on a bedside lamp, and the room's lighting changes in coordination with it.

entries.name: Intensity
entries.definition: In production conversation, the amount or strength of light. Precise records distinguish fixture output settings, illuminance reaching a surface, and luminance leaving a visible surface; these are different measurements.
entries.use: State the quantity and units when numbers matter. A dimmer percentage does not directly describe exposure or permit comparison between unrelated fixtures.
entries.example: A lighting note records 200 lux at the desk rather than calling every lamp setting “50 percent brightness.”

entries.name: Contrast
entries.definition: Difference between image regions or lighting contributions. Lighting contrast concerns illumination relationships; image contrast concerns displayed tonal or color differences after capture and processing. The same word needs its domain specified.
entries.use: Describe what is being compared and how. A stated ratio needs a measurement convention; it is not interchangeable with a software contrast-slider value.
entries.example: The crew reduces facial lighting contrast, while the colorist separately adjusts tonal contrast in the displayed image.

entries.name: Falloff
entries.definition: The reduction of illumination with distance or position within a light's coverage. For an ideal point source at constant incidence, illuminance follows an inverse-square relationship; extended sources, optics, and surroundings complicate that approximation.
entries.use: Predict how actors and backgrounds change brightness as distances change. Confirm real fixtures through measurements or tests.
entries.example: A nearby lamp lights a reader strongly but contributes much less to the wall several meters behind.

entries.name: Negative fill
entries.definition: The removal or absorption of ambient or reflected light to deepen selected shadow areas. It is often achieved with dark surfaces positioned to prevent existing light from returning to the subject.
entries.use: Increase modeling when the environment supplies more fill than desired. Negative fill changes a light relationship by subtraction rather than projecting darkness.
entries.example: Black fabric beside a pale-walled room reduces reflected light on one side of the performer's face.

entries.name: Flags
entries.definition: Opaque light-control pieces used to block illumination from selected areas or prevent unwanted light from reaching the lens. A flag's position, size, and relationship to the source determine its effect.
entries.use: Control spill, shape a lit region, or reduce flare. Flags are not the same as translucent diffusion or partial-transmission nets.
entries.example: A flag prevents a window-motivated fixture from washing out the dark noticeboard behind an actor.

entries.name: Diffusion
entries.definition: In lighting control, scattering material or an arrangement used to change the distribution and effective emitting area of a source. This differs from diffusion filters placed in the camera's optical path.
entries.use: Select material, illuminated area, and distance together. A material label alone does not specify softness, transmission, or how evenly the surface is filled.
entries.example: A large illuminated diffusion frame supplies a broad source for two people moving around a table.

entries.name: Color temperature
entries.definition: A description of light color related to a thermal radiator, expressed in kelvin (K); many nonthermal sources use correlated color temperature, or CCT. Lower values generally appear warmer and higher values cooler. [ETC, color temperature and CCT](https://blog.etcconnect.com/a-quick-definition-of-color-temperature-and-cct).
entries.use: Describe white-light balance while recognizing that CCT alone does not specify spectrum or color rendering.
entries.example: A 3200 K source appears warmer than a 5600 K source under the same camera white balance.

entries.name: Tint
entries.definition: In lighting and white-balance controls, adjustment commonly associated with the green-magenta direction, distinct from the warm-cool temperature control. The numerical scale and exact behavior depend on the fixture, camera, or software.
entries.use: Match or deliberately separate sources whose CCT values alone appear similar. Record the control system with any numeric setting.
entries.example: A slightly green office fixture is balanced against a cleaner-looking nearby lamp before filming a neutral reference.

entries.name: Palette
entries.definition: The selected colors and their relative presence across a shot, scene, or work. The final palette results from designed surfaces, illumination, capture, and grading rather than belonging to one department alone.
entries.use: Coordinate recurring colors and meaningful exceptions. Separate an intended palette from a sampled frame that also contains incidental colors.
entries.example: A blue-gray station interior allows a small red scarf to remain a recurring point of recognition.

entries.name: Saturation
entries.definition: A description of color's strength relative to a neutral appearance, with exact numerical definitions depending on the color model. Saturation is distinct from hue and brightness, though image-processing controls can interact.
entries.use: Compare muted and vivid treatments without assuming a universal scale. Check important materials and skin under the actual output transform.
entries.example: A grade reduces the intensity of background advertisements while preserving the traveler's yellow raincoat.

entries.name: Hue
entries.definition: The color-family attribute through which a color is described as red, orange, green, blue, and so on. Hue differs from saturation and lightness; numeric angles require a specified color model.
entries.use: Describe the direction of a color change precisely. A hue adjustment can target a particular region without requiring all colors to change equally.
entries.example: A slightly cyan painted door is adjusted toward blue to match adjacent shots.

entries.name: Color separation
entries.definition: Distinction between subjects or image regions achieved through differences in color. Here it means visual differentiation, not the separate color records used in printing or older photographic processes.
entries.use: Improve the readability of overlapping forms through hue, saturation, and tonal relationships. Color separation can be subtle and need not use complementary colors.
entries.example: A desaturated green coat remains distinguishable from a warmer gray wall despite similar brightness.

entries.name: Color grade
entries.definition: The coordinated treatment of image color and tone to achieve continuity and a chosen appearance. Grading can involve overall and selective adjustments; “color correction” often overlaps rather than naming a universally separate stage.
entries.use: Shape the final image while respecting capture limits and display transforms. Grade decisions cannot reconstruct detail that was never recorded.
entries.example: Exterior shots filmed under changing clouds are balanced before a shared cool-shadow treatment is applied.

entries.name: Monochrome
entries.definition: An image organized around one color family and its tonal variations, including neutral black-and-white imagery. Monochrome is not the same as simply reducing saturation a little.
entries.use: Emphasize luminance structure, texture, or a constrained color approach. Conversion choices determine how originally different colors separate as tones.
entries.example: In a black-and-white sequence, the grade distinguishes a red sign from green foliage through their resulting gray values.

entries.name: Cut
entries.definition: An immediate change from one shot to another, with no visible transitional overlap. The sound may change at the same moment or follow a separate edit point.
entries.use: Choose the cut point around a movement, look, idea, or change in attention. A cut can feel unobtrusive or emphatic depending on the relationship between the images.
entries.example: A mechanic notices a vibration; the film cuts directly to the loose bolt causing it.

entries.name: Dissolve
entries.definition: A transition in which the outgoing image gradually becomes transparent while the incoming image becomes visible, temporarily placing both images together. “Cross dissolve” is a common name for this overlap.
entries.use: Consider the combined image as well as the endpoints. Duration, alignment, and contrast can suggest passage, association, or lingering memory without automatically specifying elapsed time.
entries.example: A lit apartment dissolves into the same room after sunrise, with the window remaining aligned.

entries.name: Fade
entries.definition: A gradual transition between an image and a uniform field, often black. A fade-out removes the image; a fade-in introduces it. Unlike a dissolve, two scene images need not overlap.
entries.use: Mark a boundary, an interruption, or a change in attention. Specify the field color and whether sound continues, since those choices alter the perceived closure.
entries.example: The workshop fades to black while its final machine hum continues for another second.

entries.name: Wipe
entries.definition: A transition in which a moving boundary progressively replaces one image with another. The boundary may be straight, shaped, soft, or motivated by an object crossing the frame.
entries.use: Specify direction, speed, edge treatment, and the relationship to movement inside the shots. A wipe can announce a chapter or connect coordinated movement.
entries.example: A passing bus fills the frame, and its trailing edge reveals the destination street.

entries.name: Match cut
entries.definition: A cut that connects shots through a salient similarity, such as shape, position, movement, or conceptual association. It need not preserve continuous action or connect adjacent places.
entries.use: Name the feature being matched and the meaning created by the change. Do not use the label for every smooth edit; match on action is a more specific continuity technique.
entries.example: A circular ventilation fan cuts to an overhead view of a spinning pottery wheel.

entries.name: Jump cut
entries.definition: A cut that creates a noticeable discontinuity within a similar view of the same subject, often by removing part of an action or interval. The subject appears to jump in position or time.
entries.use: Compress repetition, expose editing, or produce deliberate restlessness. Check whether the jump communicates the intended omission rather than accidentally confusing the action.
entries.example: Three cuts within a fixed view show a painter repeatedly changing the color of one wall.

entries.name: Smash cut
entries.definition: An abrupt cut emphasizing a strong contrast between adjacent moments, often in sound, scale, action, or emotional tone. It describes the force of the juxtaposition rather than a separate transition mechanism.
entries.use: Build a clear expectation before disrupting it. Loudness alone does not make a contrast meaningful, and a quiet incoming shot can be equally forceful.
entries.example: A crowd celebrates a promised launch; the next image is a deserted, silent factory floor.

entries.name: Continuity editing
entries.definition: An approach that helps viewers understand a coherent flow of action, space, and time across shots. It uses cues such as consistent direction, matching actions, and intelligible looks, while often omitting unimportant intervals.
entries.use: Decide which relationships viewers must understand, then preserve the cues supporting them. Continuity is an organized impression, not a requirement to show every movement.
entries.example: A worker enters a room, approaches a desk, and opens a drawer across three compatible angles.

entries.name: Discontinuity editing
entries.definition: An approach that foregrounds interruptions or inconsistencies in spatial, temporal, graphic, or narrative flow. It can deliberately prevent the seamless connections associated with continuity editing.
entries.use: Identify what the interruption should make viewers notice or question. A deliberate discontinuity still benefits from a clear intention and enough context to support interpretation.
entries.example: A discussion repeatedly returns to an empty chair from incompatible angles, interrupting the otherwise stable room geography.

entries.name: Cross-cutting
entries.definition: Alternation between distinct lines of action, often in different locations and often understood as simultaneous. Its relationship to “parallel editing” varies among writers and production teams.
entries.use: State explicitly whether the actions share a time, cause one another, or only resemble one another. The switching pattern can imply a connection that the story later confirms or complicates.
entries.example: A technician restores power while passengers wait in the stalled elevator served by that circuit.

entries.name: Parallel editing
entries.definition: Alternating or juxtaposing lines of action to establish a relationship between them. It is often used interchangeably with cross-cutting; some traditions distinguish the terms by simultaneity or thematic comparison.
entries.use: Describe the actual temporal and thematic relationship instead of depending on a disputed boundary. This wiki keeps both labels searchable without treating one definition as universal.
entries.example: Preparations for a public banquet alternate with a family dividing a small evening meal.

entries.name: Montage
entries.definition: The construction of meaning through the arrangement and juxtaposition of shots. In common production shorthand, a “montage sequence” often means a condensed series showing a process or passage of time; theoretical uses are broader.
entries.use: Specify whether the intention is compression, comparison, accumulation, or collision between ideas. A music track is optional.
entries.example: Repeated images of measuring, cutting, and repairing compress several weeks of building a small boat.

entries.name: Shot/reverse shot
entries.definition: An alternating pattern of views toward opposing sides of an interaction, commonly two people speaking or looking at one another. The shots need not have identical framing or show literal opposites.
entries.use: Control whose experience dominates through duration, framing, and when reactions replace speech. Maintain readable relationships unless disorientation serves a specific purpose.
entries.example: A tenant explains a problem in medium close-up; the reverse view holds on the landlord's delayed response.

entries.name: Eyeline match
entries.definition: An edit linking a person's look with a following image understood as what they are looking toward. Direction and angle help establish the spatial relationship, even when the shots were filmed separately.
entries.use: Check gaze height, screen position, and the implied distance to the object. A following view can suggest attention without necessarily becoming a literal optical point-of-view shot.
entries.example: A child looks upward and right; the next image shows a kite caught above the doorway.

entries.name: Match on action
entries.definition: A cut between views that carries an action across the edit with compatible movement and timing. The viewer follows the action rather than being distracted by the camera change.
entries.use: Compare body position, object state, movement direction, and the precise phase of the gesture. A tiny timing adjustment may feel smoother than mechanically identical frames.
entries.example: A hand begins opening a case in a wide shot and completes the movement in close-up.

entries.name: Screen direction
entries.definition: The direction a person, object, or look appears to travel or face within the image, such as left to right. It is a screen relationship, not necessarily a fixed compass direction.
entries.use: Preserve direction when it helps viewers follow a route, pursuit, or exchange. Establish a visible turn or new orientation when direction changes.
entries.example: A courier continues moving left to right across three street views until a clear turn reverses the route.

entries.name: 180-degree rule
entries.definition: A continuity guideline that keeps camera positions on one side of an established axis of action, helping preserve relative screen positions and directions. The axis may connect people or follow movement.
entries.use: Draw the axis before choosing coverage. Crossing it can work when movement, a new establishing view, or deliberate disorientation makes the change understandable.
entries.example: Two negotiators remain on opposite screen sides until a visible camera move circles behind one of them.

entries.name: J-cut
entries.definition: A split edit in which incoming audio starts before the corresponding incoming image. The next shot or scene is therefore heard while the previous image is still visible.
entries.use: Lead attention toward a new speaker, place, or event. Decide how much the early sound reveals and whether it should first be interpreted as belonging to the outgoing image.
entries.example: Train wheels become audible over a sleeping passenger's home before the picture changes to the station.

entries.name: L-cut
entries.definition: A split edit in which outgoing audio continues after the image changes to the next shot. The earlier sound remains present while viewers receive new visual information.
entries.use: Hold a thought across a reaction or scene change. Check whether the overlapping voice is continuing live dialogue, remembered speech, or an editorial connection.
entries.example: An engineer keeps explaining a fault while the image cuts from her face to the damaged assembly.

entries.name: Sound bridge
entries.definition: Sound that connects adjacent shots or scenes across a visual boundary, through continuation, anticipation, or an associated sonic element. J-cuts and L-cuts are specific ways to create such a connection.
entries.use: Decide whether the bridge preserves a shared space or connects different times and places. Document where the sound belongs within the story.
entries.example: Rain continues across a cut from a courtyard to the room overlooking it, maintaining the same storm.

entries.name: Insert
entries.definition: A shot emphasizing a detail within the principal action or scene, commonly a hand, object, display, or written information. Its function is to make a relevant element available to attention.
entries.use: Establish enough context for the detail to be understood and allow enough time for any required reading. An insert need not always be an extreme close-up.
entries.example: During a repair, an insert reveals that the replacement component carries the wrong serial number.

entries.name: Cutaway
entries.definition: A shot that temporarily leaves the main action for a related subject, reaction, or surrounding detail. It may supply context, redirect attention, or provide room to omit part of the principal action.
entries.use: Check what viewers infer about simultaneity and location. The distinction from an insert is functional and can vary with how a scene is organized.
entries.example: A heated meeting cuts away to an assistant waiting outside the closed door.

entries.name: Shot duration
entries.definition: The time a shot occupies in the finished sequence between its beginning and end. Duration can be measured precisely, but its experienced speed depends on activity, information, sound, and expectation.
entries.use: Record actual duration alongside the beat it must communicate. Avoid assuming that a numerical target guarantees tension, calm, or clarity.
entries.example: A six-second shot gives viewers time to notice a missing photograph before a character reacts to it.

entries.name: Cutting rate
entries.definition: The frequency of cuts across a specified interval, sometimes described as cuts per minute. It summarizes one aspect of editing pace while concealing variation within that interval.
entries.use: Define the measurement window and examine the distribution of shot lengths. Compare performance tempo and event density separately rather than treating a high rate as automatic excitement.
entries.example: The final minute doubles the number of cuts while the characters themselves become increasingly motionless.

entries.name: Hold
entries.definition: A deliberate continuation of a shot, pose, or moment beyond a point where a change might be expected. In editing discussion, “hold” usually means retaining the image rather than cutting away.
entries.use: Specify what remains active during the hold: a look, background movement, sound, or the viewer's uncertainty. Distinguish it from a literal freeze frame.
entries.example: After a visitor leaves, the shot holds on the host rearranging the untouched second cup.

entries.name: Pause
entries.definition: A temporary reduction or suspension of action, speech, or narrative progression. A pause may occur within a moving shot and can retain substantial environmental sound or visual activity.
entries.use: Locate the interruption in a particular layer and decide what viewers should process during it. Length alone does not establish whether the pause feels reflective or uncomfortable.
entries.example: A witness stops speaking while traffic continues behind her, leaving the unfinished sentence unresolved.

entries.name: Ellipsis
entries.definition: The omission of part of an event or time interval from the presentation, allowing viewers to infer what occurred between the shown moments. It can be brief or span years.
entries.use: Preserve the information needed to understand the change while deciding what remains uncertain. A cut, dissolve, title, or sound transition may carry the omission.
entries.example: A baker starts kneading dough; the next shot shows the cooled loaves being packed for delivery.

entries.name: Repetition
entries.definition: The return of an image, action, sound, or structural unit within a sequence. Repetition can recreate the same material or show a recurring event with meaningful changes.
entries.use: Identify what stays stable and what changes at each recurrence. The audience learns a pattern, so even a small variation can become significant.
entries.example: Three mornings begin with the same doorway composition; on the fourth, the expected person never enters.

entries.name: Rhythmic pattern
entries.definition: An organized relationship among durations, accents, movements, and intervals across time. Editing rhythm can align with speech or music, work independently, or repeatedly shift between them.
entries.use: Describe the pattern in concrete terms, such as short–short–long or alternating impact and recovery. Test it with and without music to locate its actual source.
entries.example: Two brief preparation shots precede a longer attempt, and that three-part pattern repeats with increasing strain.

entries.name: Long take
entries.definition: A shot sustained for an unusually extended duration relative to its context, without an apparent cut. There is no universal number of seconds that makes a take “long.”
entries.use: Plan how attention develops inside the image through performance, blocking, movement, or changing information. A long take can contain rapid action and need not produce a slow experience.
entries.example: One uninterrupted view follows a cook managing several simultaneous orders during a crowded service.

entries.name: Sequence shot
entries.definition: A shot that carries the dramatic work of a whole scene or substantial sequence within a continuous presentation. It is often a long take, but its defining emphasis is structural completeness.
entries.use: Identify the beginning, developments, and resolution that must occur inside the shot. Specify if the intended continuous appearance is assembled with concealed cuts.
entries.example: One moving shot follows an inspection from arrival through discovery of the fault to the decision to close the building.

entries.name: Accelerated montage
entries.definition: A montage whose succession of images becomes progressively faster, commonly through decreasing shot durations. “Accelerated” here describes the editing pattern rather than necessarily speeding up the footage itself.
entries.use: Set a perceivable baseline before increasing frequency, and retain enough information for the actions to register. Sound accents can support or resist the acceleration.
entries.example: Packing shots shorten as a departure approaches, ending on one sustained view of an item left behind.

entries.name: Dialogue
entries.definition: Speech exchanged by people or characters within a scene, including conversation carried through devices or heard outside the frame. Dialogue describes the dramatic function, not the method used to record it.
entries.use: Plan intelligibility, overlap, interruption, and the relationship between words and reactions. A dialogue track may combine production recordings, alternate takes, and replacement recordings.
entries.example: Two coworkers discuss a missing shipment while a radio operator interrupts with a contradictory delivery time.

entries.name: Production sound
entries.definition: Audio recorded during the filming of a scene, including dialogue, actions, and the surrounding environment. It may be synchronized with the camera recording or captured separately during the same production setting.
entries.use: Identify which elements are usable, which carry valuable performance, and which need support in post-production. Preserve take and microphone information so matching remains possible.
entries.example: The location recording retains an actor's hesitant delivery, while an intrusive generator hum is reduced during editing.

entries.name: ADR
entries.definition: Automated dialogue replacement: recording dialogue after filming to replace or supplement lines, usually while matching the pictured performance. “Looping” is a common related production name. Despite “automated,” performance and synchronization require creative work.
entries.use: Address unusable audio or changed lines while matching timing, delivery, and acoustic perspective. ADR is not a general name for all voiceover.
entries.example: An actor rerecords one sentence obscured by a passing truck, matching the original breath and visible mouth movement.

entries.name: Voiceover
entries.definition: Speech presented as a separate vocal layer over images, rather than an unseen speaker's live contribution to the depicted exchange. It may convey narration, remembered speech, or inner reflection.
entries.use: Specify speaker, temporal position, knowledge, and whether characters hear the voice. Do not assume that recording speech in a booth determines its narrative category.
entries.example: A traveler describes an earlier misunderstanding while the image shows the journey that produced it.

entries.name: Narration
entries.definition: The act of presenting or organizing a story or account. In sound planning, narration usually means a voice that explains, recounts, or guides interpretation, whether spoken by a participant or an external narrator.
entries.use: Establish what the narrator knows, when they know it, and how trustworthy or limited their account is. Narration can accompany evidence without settling its interpretation.
entries.example: A researcher identifies dates over archive images, then clearly separates a personal inference from the surviving records.

entries.name: Foley
entries.definition: Sound performed and recorded to accompany pictured actions, often footsteps, clothing movement, and object handling. Foley is a sound-effects practice distinguished by performance to the action rather than simply selecting an existing recording.
entries.use: Match gesture, material, weight, and perspective while deciding which details deserve emphasis. The performed source may differ from the object depicted.
entries.example: A Foley performer recreates cautious footsteps and a stiff coat's movement for a character entering an empty office.

entries.name: Sound effects
entries.definition: Constructed or selected sonic elements representing actions, objects, environments, or imagined events beyond dialogue and music. They may come from original recordings, libraries, synthesis, processing, or combinations of these methods.
entries.use: Define the event and its narrative importance before choosing a recognizable or abstract sound. Separate dramatic emphasis from a claim of literal acoustic realism.
entries.example: A fictional scanner combines a motor click, filtered breath, and a short electronic pulse into one designed event.

entries.name: Ambience
entries.definition: The surrounding sonic environment that establishes a place, time, or atmosphere, often through sustained or recurring background elements. Ambience may include weather, traffic, machinery, animals, or distant human activity.
entries.use: Build spatial and temporal consistency while selecting details that support the scene. Ambient layers can change gradually without becoming the main event.
entries.example: A harbor scene contains distant engines, water against pilings, intermittent gulls, and a faint public-address system.

entries.name: Room tone
entries.definition: The relatively steady background sound of a particular recording space under its actual recording conditions, captured without intended dialogue or prominent action. It is not digital silence and is narrower than a complete designed ambience.
entries.use: Smooth dialogue edits and fill gaps without suddenly changing the acoustic bed. Match the relevant setup and listen for conspicuous repeated noises when looping.
entries.example: A short clean recording of an office's ventilation fills the gap between two edited interview answers.

entries.name: Diegetic sound
entries.group: Relationship to the story and image
entries.definition: Sound presented as belonging to the world of the story: a voice, machine, instrument, or other source that exists there. The source may be visible or outside the frame.
entries.use: Record the represented source independently from recording method and screen visibility. A studio-created effect can represent a diegetic event just as a location recording can.
entries.example: A telephone rings in the next room while the camera remains on someone deciding whether to answer.

entries.name: Nondiegetic sound
entries.group: Relationship to the story and image
entries.definition: Sound presented from outside the story world's immediate events, such as dramatic underscoring or an external commentary. “Non-diegetic” is an equivalent spelling; an unseen source alone does not establish this category.
entries.use: Specify how the sound addresses the audience and whether its status changes during the sequence. Avoid classifying every voiceover or musical passage automatically.
entries.example: An orchestral swell accompanies an isolated swimmer although no musical source exists in the represented location.

entries.name: On-screen sound
entries.group: Relationship to the story and image
entries.definition: Sound whose represented source is visible in the current image. This label describes visibility, not whether the final recording was made during filming or added later.
entries.use: Check synchronization and the relationship between visible action and heard emphasis. A visible source may remain quiet in a subjective mix, so visibility does not require prominence.
entries.example: A teacup visibly touches a saucer and a carefully timed contact sound makes the nervous movement noticeable.

entries.name: Off-screen sound
entries.group: Relationship to the story and image
entries.definition: Sound whose represented source lies outside the current frame while remaining part of the scene or story space. It can establish activity that viewers have not yet seen.
entries.use: Define the implied direction, distance, and source identity. Off-screen sound and nondiegetic sound answer different questions and should not be used as interchangeable labels.
entries.example: Keys turn in a lock behind the camera while the image stays on a person hiding a letter.

entries.name: Subjective sound
entries.group: Relationship to the story and image
entries.definition: Sound organized to express a particular person's perception, attention, memory, or internal experience rather than a neutral presentation of the environment. It may alter level, clarity, space, or the selection of audible events.
entries.use: Identify whose experience governs the mix and how viewers recognize that shift. Subjectivity does not require every external sound to disappear.
entries.example: During an anxious wait, a clock grows prominent while nearby conversation becomes difficult to distinguish.

entries.name: Sound perspective
entries.definition: The perceived relationship between listener and sound source, including distance, direction, obstruction, and acoustic space. Loudness contributes, but clarity, frequency balance, reverberation, and spatial placement also shape the impression.
entries.use: Decide whether the listening position follows the camera, a character, or a dramatic emphasis. Check transitions as sources move or shots change.
entries.example: A voice becomes muffled and less direct when the character speaking closes a heavy door between rooms.

entries.name: Dynamic range
entries.definition: The span between quieter and louder portions of an audio signal or program, with the exact measurement depending on the chosen method. It differs from simply making the whole mix louder.
entries.use: Plan contrast around intelligibility and the intended listening environment. Record any technical measurement separately from the creative note, since peaks and perceived loudness are not identical.
entries.example: A restrained interior mix leaves room for a sudden door slam to feel sharply louder.

entries.name: Layering
entries.definition: Combining multiple audio elements so they operate as a coordinated sound or environment. Layers can contribute separate roles such as impact, texture, scale, movement, or emotional association.
entries.use: Give each layer a purpose and check the result with layers muted individually. Additional tracks can obscure dialogue or blur an effect instead of strengthening it.
entries.example: A large gate uses a low mechanical strain, a brief latch click, and scattered metal vibrations.

entries.name: Silence
entries.definition: An absence or substantial reduction of expected sound. Filmic silence may retain breath or room tone; literal digital silence is only one possible implementation.
entries.use: State which layers disappear and which remain. The impact depends on the preceding sound and on the audience's expectation, not solely on a low level reading.
entries.example: Music and street ambience drop away after an unwelcome announcement, leaving only a person's uneven breathing.

entries.name: Reverberation
entries.definition: The dense persistence of reflected sound after its initial arrival, contributing to the impression of an acoustic space. It differs from a clearly separated echo, although the two can coexist.
entries.use: Match decay, early reflections, and the balance of direct and reflected sound to the intended space or subjective treatment. More reverb does not simply mean “farther away.”
entries.example: A short shout lingers in a stairwell after the speaker has moved out of sight.

entries.name: Distortion
entries.definition: An alteration of a signal's waveform that changes its sonic character, often adding roughness or additional frequency content. It can result from unwanted overload or be deliberately introduced as an effect.
entries.use: Identify whether the distortion represents a device, a damaged recording, or a perceptual state. Preserve intelligibility when the words or event remain necessary.
entries.example: A strained loudspeaker breaks up at vocal peaks while an announcement remains understandable enough to guide the crowd.

entries.name: Sound bridge
entries.definition: A sound connection across a picture edit, joining shots or scenes through a continuing or anticipated element. Its function concerns the relationship across the boundary rather than a particular kind of sound.
entries.use: Mark the visual cut separately from audio start and end points. Explain whether the bridge implies continuous space, memory, association, or a transition into another location.
entries.example: The rhythm of a workshop machine continues over the first image of a worker's train ride home.

entries.name: Score
entries.definition: Music composed or arranged to support a film's dramatic structure, commonly heard as nondiegetic accompaniment. The term can also refer to the written musical notation, so production context matters.
entries.use: Describe what the music should contribute: perspective, structure, anticipation, ambiguity, or emotional emphasis. Specify where it enters, changes, and stops rather than asking only for a mood.
entries.example: A sparse score introduces a new harmonic layer only when a character decides to enter the abandoned building.

entries.name: Source music
entries.definition: Music presented as coming from a source within the story world, such as a radio, performance, or headphones. It is diegetic music whether or not that source is currently visible.
entries.use: Establish the source and its acoustic perspective. If the presentation expands into underscoring, describe the transition instead of forcing the entire passage into one category.
entries.example: A small radio plays in a kitchen, becoming muffled when the scene moves into the hallway.

entries.name: Cue
entries.definition: A specified musical or sound passage associated with a production moment, commonly identified by an entry point, exit point, and purpose. “Cue” can also mean the trigger instructing that passage to begin.
entries.use: Give the cue an identifier and describe required synchronization points without prescribing every musical detail. Distinguish temporary reference music from the intended final cue.
entries.example: Cue M12 begins after a nod, supports the walk outside, and ends before the next conversation.

entries.name: Theme
entries.definition: A recognizable musical idea capable of returning or being developed across a work. It may be melodic, harmonic, or rhythmic and need not always represent a specific character.
entries.use: Describe its identity and how changes in context or arrangement affect its meaning. Avoid confusing a musical theme with the film's broader thematic subject.
entries.example: A simple four-note idea first accompanies exploration, then returns more slowly during a return to the same place.

entries.name: Leitmotif
entries.definition: A recurring musical idea associated with a particular character, object, place, relationship, or concept. Its recurrence and transformation help audiences recognize connections, sometimes before those connections become visible.
entries.use: Define the association and decide how explicit it should become. A leitmotif can be brief and does not need to form a complete melody.
entries.example: A distinctive three-note figure appears whenever an absent mentor's influence affects the protagonist's decisions.

entries.name: Drone
entries.definition: A sustained or continually recurring tone, cluster, or relatively stable sonic texture that forms a prolonged musical foundation. A drone may evolve in timbre without becoming a sequence of distinct melodic gestures.
entries.use: Specify tonal stability, texture, movement, and duration. A drone can suggest stillness or pressure; the effect depends on its context and treatment.
entries.example: A low, slowly changing tone underlies a nighttime inspection without marking every step or cut.

entries.name: Ostinato
entries.definition: A repeated musical pattern, often rhythmic or melodic, maintained across a passage. Unlike a sustained drone, an ostinato usually has a recognizable sequence of attacks or notes that returns.
entries.use: Describe the pattern's length, instrumentation, and relationship to changing harmony or action. Repetition can create stability, insistence, or propulsion without changing tempo.
entries.example: A repeating five-note keyboard figure continues while additional instruments enter during an increasingly complex preparation sequence.

entries.name: Sting
entries.definition: A short, pointed musical or sonic accent that highlights a revelation, interruption, transition, or other moment. It is typically more concentrated than a cue supporting an extended passage.
entries.use: Choose its timing and intensity carefully so it directs attention without explaining more than intended. A sting can be comic, ominous, surprising, or restrained.
entries.example: A brief metallic chord accompanies the discovery that a supposedly empty locker contains a fresh uniform.

entries.name: Tempo
entries.definition: The speed of a musical pulse, commonly described in beats per minute or with verbal indications. Perceived activity can change independently through note density, accents, instrumentation, or the absence of an obvious pulse.
entries.use: Specify the relevant beat unit and whether tempo remains stable. Do not substitute a faster tempo for a clear description of dramatic urgency.
entries.example: Music holds at the same tempo while shorter note values make the approach to a deadline feel busier.

entries.name: Rhythm
entries.definition: The organization of sound events and silences through time, including duration, accent, recurrence, and grouping. Rhythm exists in dialogue and effects as well as music and need not maintain a regular beat.
entries.use: Identify which layer supplies the pattern and how other layers respond. Describe a relation such as syncopation or interruption through a playable example.
entries.example: Uneven hammer blows gradually settle into a repeating pattern that the musical percussion later adopts.

entries.name: Timbre
entries.definition: The character or tone quality that helps distinguish sounds with similar pitch and loudness. Timbre develops through spectral content, attack, decay, noise, articulation, and changes across the sound's duration.
entries.use: Pair descriptive words with listening examples, since “warm,” “thin,” or “metallic” can mean different things to collaborators. Identify the feature that matters.
entries.example: The same melody played on breathy flute and muted electronic tones suggests two different qualities of intimacy.

entries.name: Instrumentation
entries.definition: The selection and combination of instruments or sound-producing sources used in a musical arrangement. It concerns which voices are available and how their roles are distributed.
entries.use: Describe register, density, articulation, and interaction alongside instrument names. A small ensemble can sound forceful, and an orchestra can play with great restraint.
entries.example: A cue uses low clarinet for sustained movement, plucked strings for intermittent detail, and no percussion.

entries.name: Dissonance
entries.definition: A relationship among pitches experienced or treated as unstable, tense, or demanding continuation within a musical context. Its character depends on tuning, register, timbre, style, and listening conventions; it is not simply a synonym for unpleasant sound.
entries.use: Describe the intended tension and whether it resolves, persists, or becomes familiar through repetition.
entries.example: Two close sustained pitches gradually separate as a character's conflicting choices become clearer.

entries.name: Consonance
entries.definition: A relationship among pitches experienced or treated as relatively stable or settled within a musical context. Historical and stylistic conventions influence that interpretation; consonance does not automatically imply happiness or agreement.
entries.use: Specify whether stability offers rest, reassurance, ritual, or unsettling emotional distance. Its dramatic effect depends on surrounding sound and images.
entries.example: A settled chord remains beneath an unresolved argument, making the music's composure feel detached from the people.

entries.name: Musical counterpoint
entries.definition: In music, the interaction of distinct melodic lines that retain some independence. In film discussion, “counterpoint” also describes music whose character contrasts with the image rather than simply reinforcing its apparent mood.
entries.use: State which meaning is intended. For picture–music contrast, explain the resulting perspective instead of assuming that any mismatch is meaningful.
entries.example: A buoyant mechanical tune accompanies monotonous assembly work, suggesting the institution's optimism rather than the workers' feelings.

entries.name: 2D animation
entries.definition: Animation built primarily from two-dimensional drawings, shapes, images, or rigs. It can be drawn frame by frame, assembled from moving parts, or combined with depth cues and three-dimensional elements.
entries.use: Specify line behavior, pose changes, texture, and how forms turn or overlap. “2D” identifies a construction approach, not a single visual style or a guarantee of flat-looking space.
entries.example: Paperlike characters move through painted backgrounds while their facial expressions change through replacement drawings.

entries.name: 3D animation
entries.definition: Animation using objects and cameras represented in three-dimensional space, usually within a digital scene. Geometry, rigging, materials, lighting, and rendering together produce the final image, which may appear realistic or strongly graphic.
entries.use: Separate movement decisions from rendering style. A three-dimensional model can use stepped poses, painted textures, and simplified lighting rather than smooth naturalistic motion.
entries.example: A modeled delivery robot moves with abrupt pose changes and renders with broad inklike outlines.

entries.name: Stop motion
entries.definition: Animation created by physically adjusting objects between separately photographed frames. Puppets, clay, cutouts, everyday objects, or other materials can be animated this way; digital finishing may still be part of the process.
entries.use: Plan stable registration, controllable lighting, object support, and the size of each movement. Material changes and imperfections can be retained as expressive qualities.
entries.example: A folded-paper bird advances across a miniature desk through small physical adjustments between exposures.

entries.name: Rotoscoping
entries.definition: Tracing or interpreting recorded movement frame by frame to create animation, or isolating pictured elements with evolving masks in effects work. These related uses share frame-specific reference but serve different production purposes.
entries.use: State whether the task is performance-based animation or matte creation. Decide how much timing, contour, and detail should follow the recorded source.
entries.example: An animator redraws a dancer with simplified shapes while preserving the measured changes in balance from a filmed performance.

entries.name: Motion capture
entries.definition: Recording movement data from a performer or object for use in animation or analysis. Systems vary, and the resulting data usually requires interpretation, cleanup, retargeting, or additional animation for the final character.
entries.use: Define which motion is captured and how the target body's proportions differ. Do not equate captured movement with a finished animated performance.
entries.example: A performer's cautious walk supplies a starting motion that animators adjust for a much longer-legged fictional creature.

entries.name: Key pose
entries.definition: A significant body or object configuration that communicates an action's intention, structure, or dramatic beat. A key pose is a visual idea; a software keyframe is a stored property value and need not represent an important pose.
entries.use: Check silhouette, balance, direction of force, and readability before refining intermediate motion.
entries.example: Three key poses show a figure noticing a heavy box, committing to lift it, and failing to straighten fully.

entries.name: Timing
entries.definition: The placement and duration of actions, poses, and changes across frames or seconds. Timing determines when something happens and how long it lasts, while spacing describes the positional change between successive images.
entries.use: Set the main beats before refining motion curves. A longer hesitation can alter intention even when the physical path remains identical.
entries.example: A character reaches for a handle, waits twelve frames, then pulls, making the decision feel considered.

entries.name: Spacing
entries.definition: The differences in position or shape between successive displayed states of an animation. With timing held constant, closely grouped positions suggest slower motion and wider gaps suggest faster motion.
entries.use: Inspect frame sequences or motion paths to shape acceleration, deceleration, and impact. Equal overall duration does not imply equal movement character.
entries.example: A rolling coin covers larger distances early in a one-second move and progressively smaller distances as it settles.

entries.name: Anticipation
entries.definition: A preparatory action or cue that helps establish an upcoming movement or event. It can involve body movement, a look, a change of pose, or a brief pause that directs attention.
entries.use: Adjust how much warning viewers need and how the preparation expresses intention. Omitting or minimizing anticipation may be appropriate for surprise or a mechanical style.
entries.example: Before pushing a stuck cabinet, a character plants one foot and shifts their shoulders toward it.

entries.name: Follow-through
entries.definition: Continued movement after the principal action changes or stops, often visible in flexible parts, clothing, or attached objects. It helps communicate inertia and material behavior, with the amount depending on the chosen style.
entries.use: Identify which parts lead, lag, and settle rather than applying the same delay everywhere. Follow-through should support the main action's readability.
entries.example: A courier stops abruptly, but the loose strap of a shoulder bag swings forward and settles afterward.

entries.name: Squash and stretch
entries.definition: Deliberate deformation that compresses or extends a form to communicate flexibility, force, weight, or expression. Maintaining apparent volume is a common guiding choice, but stylization can intentionally depart from it.
entries.use: Match the amount and location of deformation to the material and performance. Rigid objects may rely on pose and timing instead of visible deformation.
entries.example: A soft toy compresses against a tabletop, then lengthens briefly as a child pulls it upward.

entries.name: Practical effects
entries.definition: Effects physically produced during filming, such as controlled atmospheric effects, mechanical movement, makeup effects, or constructed action elements. “Practical” describes an on-set method, which can still be combined with extensive digital finishing.
entries.use: Specify the visible behavior and the physical interaction needed from performers, lighting, or objects. Coordinate specialist execution rather than treating a visual reference as a build procedure.
entries.example: A mechanically moving wall panel gives an actor a real surface to react to before its support is removed digitally.

entries.name: Miniatures
entries.definition: Physical scale models photographed to represent larger objects or environments. Their apparent scale depends on detail, camera placement, depth of field, lighting, movement, and how they connect to surrounding shots.
entries.use: Plan the intended viewpoint and scale cues before construction. A model's dimensions alone do not establish the size viewers perceive.
entries.example: A small industrial building model supplies a distant exterior, matched to full-size doorway footage through angle and lighting.

entries.name: Animatronics
entries.definition: Mechanically controlled figures or parts that perform movement physically in front of the camera. They can range from a moving feature to a complex creature and may be operated directly or through programmed controls.
entries.use: Identify the necessary range of expression and interaction. Coordinate the mechanism's limits with framing, performance, and any digital extensions.
entries.example: A physical creature head blinks and turns toward an actor while its larger body is completed digitally.

entries.name: Compositing
entries.definition: Combining separately created image elements into a final image or sequence. Live footage, rendered objects, paintings, text, and effects can be layered using mattes, transparency, color work, and spatial adjustments.
entries.use: Evaluate edges, occlusion, lighting, focus, motion blur, grain, and color together. A technically clean matte is only one part of a convincing composite.
entries.example: A filmed performer, a rendered structure, and a photographed sky are combined into one consistent exterior shot.

entries.name: Matte painting
entries.definition: A painted or image-based environment element used to extend or replace part of a photographed or rendered scene. Contemporary matte paintings may combine photographs, painting, and projections onto simplified geometry.
entries.use: Design for the camera's permitted movement and the required depth relationships. A convincing still background may reveal its limitations when a camera move introduces parallax.
entries.example: A modest rooftop set is extended with a distant painted city, leaving nearby railings and performers physically filmed.

entries.name: Digital environment
entries.definition: A digitally constructed setting or setting extension, potentially using geometry, textures, scans, procedural systems, and image-based elements. It may replace the entire location or supply only the portions absent from the photographed plate.
entries.use: Specify camera freedom, interactive surfaces, scale, lighting, and required detail. A digital environment is a spatial solution, not necessarily a photorealistic one.
entries.example: A warehouse interior continues beyond a built foreground into a modeled hall visible through a large doorway.

entries.name: Motion tracking
entries.definition: Analyzing motion in recorded images to estimate how a feature, surface, object, or camera moves. The resulting data can guide attachment, stabilization, replacement, or integration of new elements.
entries.use: Choose a tracking method appropriate to the motion and inspect drift, occlusion, and perspective changes. Tracking image movement is different from capturing a performer's movement as animation data.
entries.example: A tracked wall plane keeps a replacement sign aligned as a handheld camera moves through the corridor.

entries.name: Stylization
entries.definition: The deliberate shaping of appearance or movement through selected conventions rather than exhaustive imitation of observable reality. It can affect proportion, line, texture, light, timing, perspective, and the amount of detail shown.
entries.use: State a small set of repeatable choices and where exceptions belong. “Stylized” alone provides little direction because very different conventions fit the word.
entries.example: Background machinery uses simplified silhouettes while character hands retain detailed gestures needed to explain the repair.

entries.name: Integration
entries.definition: The process and perceived result of making independently produced elements belong together within a shared visual and temporal presentation. Successful integration may pursue realism or a coherent, visibly mixed aesthetic.
entries.use: Compare contact, scale, edges, light, texture, timing, and sound at actual playback speed. Decide which seams are expressive and which are unintended.
entries.example: A drawn figure retains visible pencil texture but casts a deliberately matching shadow across a photographed tabletop.

entries.name: Continuity
entries.definition: Consistency of relevant states and relationships across frames, shots, or production elements. In effects work, this includes object condition, lighting, materials, damage, motion phase, and spatial position as well as narrative facts.
entries.use: Record the states that must persist and the events that intentionally change them. Evaluate neighboring shots together rather than approving isolated images alone.
entries.example: A crack added to a digital window remains in the same place when the camera angle reverses.

entries.name: Interaction
entries.definition: The visible or audible consequences of one element affecting another, such as contact, resistance, shadow, reflection, displacement, or attention. Interaction makes a relationship legible even when its components were produced separately.
entries.use: Identify the exact contact point and expected response in each medium. Eye direction, timing, and transferred force can matter more than surface detail.
entries.example: A live-action actor lifts a digital object while the hand position, sleeve compression, and contact shadow support its weight.

entries.name: Simulation
entries.definition: Computing changing behavior from a model and its parameters, often for cloth, hair, particles, fluids, or rigid bodies. A simulation approximates selected behavior; it does not automatically produce the desired shot or establish physical truth.
entries.use: Choose conditions and constraints around the visible goal, then inspect stability and art-direct the result where necessary. Keep repeatable settings for revisions.
entries.example: A cloth simulation supplies a banner's response to wind, then selected timing is adjusted to keep an emblem readable.

entries.name: Observational approach
entries.definition: An approach emphasizing people and events unfolding before the camera, with comparatively little overt prompting or explanatory intervention in the presented scene. This is Nichols's observational mode.
entries.use: Plan patient coverage that preserves actions and relationships. Document the recording circumstances separately, since an unobtrusive presentation does not mean the filmmaker had no influence.
entries.example: A sequence follows a volunteer kitchen preparing a meal, allowing coordination and disagreement to emerge through the work itself.

entries.name: Participatory approach
entries.definition: An approach in which encounters between filmmaker and participants help generate the material and knowledge presented. This is Nichols's participatory mode; conversation, inquiry, and intervention become part of the account.
entries.use: Clarify the filmmaker's role and the conditions of the encounter. Decide which questions, responses, and power differences viewers need to understand.
entries.example: A filmmaker accompanies a resident on a walk, asking how each changed building relates to the resident's memories.

entries.name: Expository approach
entries.definition: An approach organized around an explanation or argument, commonly using commentary, testimony, and images in support. This is Nichols's expository mode; a single authoritative voice is common but not required.
entries.use: Map each assertion to relevant support and identify where interpretation enters. Let images provide meaningful evidence instead of merely decorating an already complete spoken explanation.
entries.example: A short film explains a river's changing course using dated maps, observations, and clearly attributed expert interpretation.

entries.name: Reflexive approach
